212:
I pay homage to the Buddha, who possesses the manifest Bhūtaggasayambhucakka and who taught the well-arisen knowledge to humans. In this Saddanīti treatise, I have spoken of the Bhūvādi-kaṇḍa; let those who desire their own benefit frequent this Bhūvādi-kaṇḍa.

## Thus, in the Saddanītippakaraṇa, composed for the benefit of the wise to gain proficiency in the linguistic usage of the Tipitaka together with its ninefold divisions and commentaries,
## the sixteenth chapter, named the Bhūvādi-gaṇa, adorned with fifteen sections, is completed.
## 17. Rudhādichakka
## Rudhādigaṇika

After this Bhūvādi-kaṇḍa, how shall I speak of the six groups for the benefit of the Dispensation?

The root Rudhi is in the sense of obstruction. The root Rudhi has its function in the sense of obstruction. Here, what is called āvaraṇa (obstruction) includes closing, surrounding, oppressing, or not giving for the purpose of taking; all these are appropriate. There are forms such as rundhati, rundhiti, rundhīti, rundheti, avarundheti. In the passive voice, there is: "The path is obstructed by the man" (maggo purisena rundhiyati). There are also terms such as rodha, orodha, virodha, paṭivirodha, viruddhā, paṭiviruddhā, pariruddhā. Rundhitum, parirundhitum. Rundhitvā, parirundhitvā.

Among those terms, rodha means a prison. That prison is called rodha because it obstructs and prevents the movement of beings with cruel actions who have been put inside. Orodha means the king's harem; that harem is called orodha because the women are obstructed and confined so that they cannot travel as they please. Virodha means non-conformity (opposition). Paṭivirodha means repeated non-conformity. Viruddhā means one who has reached a state of opposition.
213:
Paṭiviruddhā means one who has reached a state of opposition in the capacity of an adversary. Pariruddhā means one who is surrounded for the purpose of capture. Therefore, it is said: "Though surrounded by enemies, there being a path for escape." Avaruddhā means one who is banished.

The root muca is used in the sense of releasing (mocana). One releases a deer from a snare. Muñcanaṃ, mocanaṃ. Release from suffering is dukkhappamocanaṃ. Moca refers to the wild banana tree. Here, moca refers to the banana tree that has seeds. Muñcituṃ. Muñcitvā. In the causative (kārita), there are forms such as "moceti, mocetuṃ, mocetvā," etc.

The root rica is used in the sense of being empty or purging (virecana). Riñcati. Riñcanaṃ, virecanaṃ, vireko, virecako. Riñcituṃ. Riñcitvā.

The root sica is used in the sense of trickling or pouring (pagg haraṇa). One pours water on the ground. One anoints a son into kingship. Abhiseko. A king who has been anointed on the head is called a muddhābhisitta khattiya. It is said: "Bail out this boat, O monk; being emptied, it will go lightly for you to Nibbāna." Sittatthānaṃ. Siñcituṃ. Siñcitvā.

The root yuja is used in the sense of yoking or exertion (yoga). Yuñjati, anuyuñjati. In the passive voice, there are forms like "yuñjiyati." Some teachers desire the form "yuñjate." Yuñjanaṃ, saṃyogo, anuyogo; one who is devoted to meditation is bhāvanānuyutto. Saññogo, saññojanaṃ; the application of meaning is atthayojanā. It is said: "To the weary, a distance of one yojana is long." Yuñjituṃ, anuyuñjituṃ. Anuyuñjitvā. Yojeti. In that context, saṃyojana refers to fetters such as sensual lust (kāmarāga). A yojana is defined as:
Twelve finger-breadths are called one span (vidatthi),
Two such spans are known as one cubit (ratana).
Seven cubits are one staff (yaṭṭhi),
Twenty staffs are one usabha.
Eighty usabhas are one gāvuta,
Four gāvutas are one yojana.

The root bhuja is used in the senses of protecting (pālana) and consuming (byavaharaṇa). Pālana means protecting. Byavaharaṇa means swallowing (eating). Bhuñjati, paribhuñjati, saṃbhuñjati. One consumes with the usage of a servant. In the causative, there are forms such as "bhojeti, bhojayati," etc. Bhojanaṃ, sambhogo; one who protects the earth or 'eats' (rules) the earth is called mahibhuja.
214:
Gāmabhojaka (village headman), upabhoga (internal use/utensils), paribhoga (external use/utensils). The rice was eaten by the venerable one. If I had eaten. One who has eaten rice (odanaṃ bhutto, buttavā, buttāvī). By the power of the tumun suffix etc., forms such as 'to eat' (bhuñjituṃ), 'to use' (paribhuñjituṃ), 'to feed' (bhojetuṃ, bhojayituṃ), 'having eaten' (bhuñjitvā, bhuñjitvāna, bhuñjiya, bhuñjiyāna), 'having fed' (bhojetvā, bhojetvāna, bhojayitvā, bhojayitvāna) are distinguished by the prefix pari etc.

In the term bhuñjati, it means one eats rice, one eats food. Thus it is taught: "One chews or eats what is chewable or what is edible." Furthermore, sometimes the word 'bhuñjati' is seen even in the case of chewable food. Is it not taught: "O Great King, eat the fruits, both superior and inferior, which are like honey"? Paribhuñjati means one uses a robe, one uses alms-food, one uses medicinal requisites for the sick; it means 'one uses/indulges' (paṭisevati). For that very reason, the term 'paṭisevati' is explained with the meaning of 'paribhuñjati'. Moreover, because it is seen as 'one enjoys sensual pleasures' (kāme bhuñjati) and 'one uses and enjoys the five cords of sensual pleasure' (pañcakāmaguṇe paribhuñjati), it should be understood that the words bhuñjana and paribhuñjana have the same meaning in some places in the sense of using or indulging. Saṃbhuñjati means one enjoys together, or one lives together.

Here, a question may arise: "Venerable sir, this root bhuja is said to be in the senses of protecting (pālana) and consuming (byavaharaṇa); how can it function in so many meanings?" It is indeed possible; roots have multiple meanings (anekattha). When those roots obtain the assistance of a prefix (upasagga), they become even more varied in meaning. From here on, I will not mention the forms of the tumun suffix etc. again. I will only mention them where there is something special.

The root kati is in the sense of cutting (chedana). One cuts (kantati, vikantati). A physician who cuts out arrows (sallakatta).

The root bhidi is in the sense of breaking or splitting (vidāraṇa). One breaks (bhindati). When the future sense is to be expressed, two forms occur: 'bhejjissati' and 'bhindissati'. One is called a 'bhikkhu' because one breaks unwholesome, evil states. Therefore, it is taught:
215:
“One is not a bhikkhu merely because one begs from others. By undertaking unwholesome states that are like poison (discordant), one is not a bhikkhu merely by begging from others. In this Dispensation, whoever has discarded both merit and evil, who lives the sublime life, and who wanders reflecting on the world (the aggregates, etc.)—he alone is truly called a ‘bhikkhu’.”

This teaching was spoken with reference to the Arahant (one whose taints are destroyed). However, those who are Sekhas (trainees) and worldling monks also deserve to be called “bhikkhu” as appropriate. One is called a saṅghabhedaka because one causes a schism in the Saṅgha. Devadatta has caused a schism in the Saṅgha. Because of the sense “is split,” the derivative “bhinna” is formed. You should not split those logs. Because of the sense “one who splits,” he is called “bhettā”.

The root chidi is in the sense of making into two parts (cutting). Because of the sense “one who cuts,” he is called “chedaka” or “chettā”. It is proper to cut the hair. Because of the sense “is cut,” it is called “chinna”. Even a tree that has been cut grows again. When these two roots, bhidi and chidi, belong to the Divādi group, they produce the two active voice forms “bhijjati” (it breaks) and “chijjati” (it is cut). Therefore, the derivation should also be made by way of the active voice, such as “bhijjatīti bhinno” (that which breaks is bhinna).

The root tadi is in the sense of oppressing and disrespecting. Tandati (he oppresses, he disrespects). Tandī (laziness), taddu (itch/scabies). The itch oppresses.

The root udi is in the sense of arising and moistening. Flowing is called pasavana. Moistening is called tindatā. Undati (it flows, it moistens). Undūra (mouse), samudda (ocean).

The root vida is in the sense of obtaining. Vindati (he obtains). Govinda (the brahmin Govinda or the god Vishnu), vitti (experience/enjoyment). Here, vitti means experience or feeling (vedanā).

The root vida is in the sense of delighting. Vindati (he delights), nibbindati (he is weary of). Nibbindana (weariness). Virajjati (he becomes dispassionate). He is weary through delighting in sensual pleasures. Vitti (delight), vitta (wealth), veda (the Vedas). He obtains the knowledge of the meaning (atthaveda) and the knowledge of the text (dhammaveda).

In this context, vitti means joy (somanassa). As it was said: “O Matali, indeed delight (vitti) arises in me upon seeing the celestial realm.” Vitta refers to wealth, so called because it produces delight.
216:
The word ‘veda’ is said to mean scripture, knowledge, and joy (somanassa). In phrases such as ‘one who has reached the far shore of the three Vedas’, ‘veda’ refers to scripture. In phrases such as ‘one should know the Brahmin who has reached knowledge (vedagũ), who is possessionless and unattached to the realm of sensual existence’, ‘veda’ refers to knowledge. In phrases such as ‘those who wander in the world having arisen joy’, ‘veda’ refers to joy (somanassa).

The word ‘veda’ occurs in the sense of Vedic scripture, knowledge, and joy.
The word ‘veda’ is expressed through these various roots.

The root ‘lipa’ is used in the sense of smearing. ‘Limpati’ (he smears), ‘limpaka’ (one who smears). ‘Avalepa’ (the smearing of pride). ‘Avalepa’ is indeed ‘ahaᅅkāra’ (ego/conceit).

The root ‘lupa’ is used in the sense of cutting off (plundering). ‘Lumpati’ (he plunders). ‘Vilumpaka’ (a plunderer), ‘vilutta’ (one who is plundered), ‘vilopa’ (plundering).

A man plunders only as long as he has power.
When others plunder him, then that plunderer is himself plundered.

The root ‘pisa’ is used in the sense of powdering (grinding). ‘Piᅃsati’ (he grinds). ‘Pisaka’ (one who grinds). ‘Pisuᅇā vācā’ (slanderous speech). In the Āgama Commentary, however, it is said: ‘The speech by which one speaks of one's own dear state and the voidness (of love) of another is called slanderous speech.’ This should be understood as being stated according to etymological characteristics (the change of letters).

The root ‘hisi’ is used in the sense of harming. ‘Hiᅃsati’, ‘vihiᅃsati’ (he harms). ‘Hiᅃsaka’ (one who harms).

‘My name was Ahimsaka (Non-harmer), though I was a harmer before.
Today I am one of true name; I do not harm any living being.’

One is called ‘sĩha’ (lion) because he harms (hinsati) beings that should be harmed. The word is formed by the reversal of the initial and final letters (vipallāsa), just as it is said ‘it is called takka (buttermilk) because of its pleasing sense (kantanattha)’. ‘Vihesaka’ (one who harms), ‘vihesana’ (harming).
217:
The root ‘sumbha’ is used in the sense of striking. ‘He strikes us like cattle.’ ‘Parisumbhati’. ‘Sumbho’. These are examples from the Pali texts:

‘Striking themselves, we await the arrival of the time (of death).’

‘By seizing the hair and lifting, and by throwing down and striking on the ground, having given much suffering, he does not leave us but stays watching.’

‘I strike the ground with force.’

In other texts, other roots (of the Rudhādi group) are mentioned. They are not mentioned here because they are not appropriate for this context. Some might think here: Just as in the Bhũvādi group, roots such as ‘saki’ (in the sense of doubt) and ‘khaji’ (in the sense of limping) result in forms like ‘saᅅkati’ and ‘khajati’ due to the arrival of the niggahĩta which becomes a class-final consonant; so too in this Rudhādi group, roots such as ‘muca’ (in the sense of releasing) and ‘kati’ (in the sense of cutting) result in forms like ‘mucati’ and ‘kantati’ due to the arrival of the niggahĩta which becomes a class-final consonant. If both are formed only by the arrival of the niggahĩta, what is the difference between these roots of the Rudhādi group and those ikāranta roots of the Bhũvādi group?

In response to this question of distinction, it is said: In the Bhũvādi group, roots that have multiple vowels, no final conjunct, and are shown as ending in ‘i’ (ikāranta), when they become verbs or nouns, they are formed strictly with the arrival of the niggahĩta in both the active (suddhakattu) and causative (hetukattu) domains. The formation of these roots is never seen anywhere without the arrival of the niggahĩta. For example: ‘saᅅkati’, ‘saᅅkā’, ‘khajati’, ‘khajo’, etc. This is the distinction of the multi-voweled ikāranta roots belonging to the Bhũvādi group.

As for the roots in the Rudhādi group that have multiple vowels, no final conjunct, and are shown as ending in ‘a’ (akāranta) or ‘u’ (ukāranta), when they become verbs, they are formed strictly with the arrival of the niggahĩta only in the active (suddhakattu) domain, but not in the causative (hetukattu) domain. When they become nouns, however, they are formed both with and without the arrival of the niggahĩta.
218:
Where forms are produced without the arrival of the niggahīta augment, they occur only as forms with a conjunct. 

How is this so? Muñcati, muñcāpeti, moceti, mocāpeti, chindāpeti, chedeti, chedāpeti, chindanaṃ, chedo, muñcanaṃ, mocanaṃ, kantati, kantanaṃ, sallakatto. 
"He eats the flesh of his own back, having cut (or scraped) it himself," 
and so on. In that [verse], "ukkacca" means having cut (or scraped).

"Venerable Sir, if this is so, having reached the state of being a noun or a verb, in the scope of the simple agent (suddhakattu) and the causal agent (hetukattu), should not only the roots such as saki and khaji, which definitely obtain the arrival of the niggahīta, be the roots belonging to the rudhādigaṇa? But roots such as muñca and chidi should not." (Thus it is objected).

That should not be said. Because they have the same nature as the root rudh, only the roots such as muñca and chidi should be roots belonging to the rudhādigaṇa. Why? Because just as in the forms of the root rudh such as "rundhissa, rundhayati, rundhāpeti, rundhanaṃ, rodho, virodho," two types of forms are seen by way of the arrival and non-arrival of the niggahīta, so it is with muñca, chidi, and others.

"Is it not that in the Kaccāyana grammar, the rule 'rudhādito niggahītapubbañca' was stated for the purpose of making the arrival of the niggahīta permanent?" (Thus it is objected). True, however, that rule was stated with reference only to the state of being a verbal word (ākhyātapada), not with reference to the state of being a nominal word (nāmapada). If it had been stated with reference also to the state of being a nominal word, then because of seeing forms such as "virodho," it should have been stated by inserting the word "vā" (optionally) as "rudhādito vā niggahītapubbañca"; but it was not stated by inserting the word "vā." Therefore, it is known that it was stated with reference only to the state of being a verbal word.

"Venerable Sir, if this is so, can it not be understood that this rule 'rudhādito niggahītapubbañca' was stated with reference only to the state of being a verbal word with a permanent niggahīta for roots such as saki and khaji?" (Thus it is objected). It cannot be so understood. Because roots such as saki and khaji do not have the same nature as the root rudh, the occurrence of two types of forms in the state of being a noun is impossible. Why? Because for those roots which have the nature of having two types of forms in the state of being a noun by way of the arrival and non-arrival of the niggahīta...
219:
That [having two types, with and without the arrival of the niggahīta in the state of being a noun] alone is the defining characteristic (lakkhaṇa) of those roots being in the rudhādigaṇa. That characteristic does not exist in roots such as saki and khaji. Indeed, in the state of being a noun, only one form with the arrival of the niggahīta is seen, such as "saṅkā" and "khañjo." As for roots such as "kamu padavikkhepe," although the existence of two types of forms in the state of being a noun is possible, such as "kamo, kamanaṃ, caṅkamo, caṅkamanaṃ," because the arrival of the niggahīta occurs only in the scope of reduplication (abbhāsa), that existence of two types is not the characteristic of being in the rudhādigaṇa. Therefore, excluding the arrival of the niggahīta that occurs in the scope of reduplication, whatever existence of two types there is [in non-reduplicated cases], that alone should be concluded as the characteristic of being in the rudhādigaṇa. This method is extremely subtle and should be well attended to.

These are the roots of the rudhādigaṇa seen by me in the Piṭaka according to my ability. 
Having looked for other roots in the Suttas (Piṭaka), you should accept them according to the suitability of the meaning.

## This is the Rudhādigaṇa.

## Divādigaṇa

The root divu occurs in the senses of playing, desiring victory, business (speech), brilliance, praise, desire, movement, and power. Here, playing (kīḷā) means dalliance (laḷanā) or dwelling by way of postures (vihāra). Dalliance (laḷanā) is enjoyment by way of experiencing beauty. Dwelling (vihāra) is existing by way of changing postures and so on. Desiring victory (vijigisā) is the wish to conquer. Business (byavahāra) is conventional usage, speaking, and teaching. Juti means brilliance (sobhā). Thuti means praise (thomanā). Kanti means the state of being desirable. Gati means movement (gamanaṃ). Satti means the power of capability. In these meanings, the root divu occurs. Dibbati, devo, devī, devatā.

Here, regarding "god" (deva), there are three kinds of gods: conventional gods (sammuti-deva), gods by rebirth (upapatti-deva), and gods by purity (visuddhi-deva). Among those gods, because they have been conventionally designated as "gods" by the world since the time of King Mahāsammata, kings, princes, and so on...
220:
Conventional gods (sammuti-deva) are kings, queens, princes, and so forth (so called because they have been designated as 'gods' by the people since the time of King Mahāsammata). Gods by rebirth (upapatti-deva) are those born in the celestial realms. Purified gods (visuddhi-deva) are the Arahants who have destroyed the taints (āsavas).

It has also been stated: "Conventional gods (sammuti-deva) are kings, queens, and princes. Gods by rebirth (upapatti-deva) are the earth-dwelling gods (bhummadeva) and those in the higher celestial realms. Purified gods (visuddhi-deva) are the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Arahants."

In this context, the etymological definition (nibbaccana) is as follows: They are called gods (deva) because they sport (kīḷanti) with sensual pleasures, jhānas, higher knowledges (abhiññā), and mastery over the mind, or because they dwell (viharanti) in those states. They are called gods because they go (gacchanti) to desired objects without hindrance. They are called gods because they are able (sakkonti) to accomplish whatever they wish. Alternatively, they are called gods (deva) because they are to be praised (deva-nīya/abhitthavanīya) as a refuge and a resort by those who wish to cross over various misfortunes. Or, they are called gods because they are desirable (kamanīya) due to being endowed with special beauty.

In this regard, the meanings of 'praise' and 'desirability' should be understood by way of the passive derivative (kamma-sādhana). The six meanings such as 'sporting' and so forth should be understood by way of the active derivative (kattu-sādhana). Some teachers recite: "The root divu occurs in the senses of sporting (kīḷā), desire to conquer (vijigīsā), usage/speech (vohāra), splendor (juti), praise (thuti), and going (gati)." Some omit the word 'gati' and recite 'juti-thutīsu'. Some omit the word 'thuti' and recite 'juti-gatīsu'. Some, however, also accept the root divu in the senses of 'ability' (satti), 'praise' (thuti), and 'desirability' (kamanat-tha). Therefore, the author of the Abhidhamma-Anuṭīkā stated: "Just as the word deva has the meanings of sporting, desire to conquer, usage, splendor, and going, it also has the meanings of ability, praise, and desirability, because roots have multiple meanings."

This is the individual etymological definition for the aforementioned conventional gods and others: Kings are called gods (sammuti-deva) because they sport (kīḷanti) and exercise sovereignty (issariya) in their own domain (kingdom). They are called gods because they sport with the five cords of sensual pleasure; or because they desire to conquer (vijetum-icchanti) their opponents; or because they speak (voharanti) of what is proper and improper for the world; or because they shine (jotanti) with the supreme splendor of the body; or because they are praised (thomiyanti) by those who desire their state; or because they are desired (kāmiyanti) to be seen...
221:
...Because they are endowed with special beauty, they are desired to be seen and their voices to be heard. Because they can go to any desired place without hindrance, and because they can accomplish various tasks through their endowed power, gods such as those of the Realm of the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājikā) are called 'deva' (gods).

Purified gods (visuddhi-deva) are called 'deva' because they sport with the supreme sport of jhāna; because they desire to conquer the opposition (defilements); because they teach the meanings of the aggregates (khandha), bases (āyatana), etc., which are the objects of extremely subtle and distinguished knowledge; because they shine with the light of extremely pure knowledge, being free from the stains of all defilements; because they are praised by the wise for being endowed with extremely stainless and distinguished qualities; because they are desired to be seen, heard, and honored for being the unsurpassed supreme field of merit; because they go to the great Deathless Nibbāna by a path from which there is no returning; and because they are able to establish beings in the bliss of the great Deathless Nibbāna by knowing their mental inclinations and engaging them in their own welfare.

The word 'deva' is used in the sense of 'sky' in such passages as: 'viddhe vigatavalāhake deve' (in the high sky, clear and free from clouds). It is used in the sense of 'rain' in such passages as: 'devo ca thokaṃ thokaṃ phusāyati' (and the rain falls drop by drop). It is used in the sense of 'king' (khattiya) in such passages as: 'ayañhi deva kumāro' (Your Majesty, this prince...). It is used in the sense of a 'sovereign person' in such passages as: 'ahaṃ deva sakalajambudīpe aññassa rañño santike kiñci bhayaṃ na passāmi' (Your Majesty, I see no danger from any other king in the whole of Jambudīpa). It is used in the sense of 'gods by rebirth' (upapatti-deva) in such passages as: 'pañcahi kāmaguṇehi samappito samangībhūto paricāreti devo maññe' (endowed and possessed of the five cords of sensual pleasure, he enjoys himself like a god). It is used in the sense of 'purified gods' (visuddhi-deva) in such passages as: 'devātidevaṃ naradammasārathiṃ' (the God of gods, the Charioteer of men to be tamed).

Both a king's consort and a celestial nymph are called 'devī'. She is called 'devī' because she is the wife of a god (deva). In terms of meaning, she is also called 'devī' because she sports and enjoys herself (dibbati), just as a female mendicant is called 'bhikkhunī' because she begs (bhikkhati). Accordingly, it is stated in the Vimānavatthu-Aṭṭhakathā: "She is called devī because she sports (dibbati) and plays by the power of her own merit."
222:
## Devatā
Devatā refers to a male deity (devaputta), a Brahmā, or a female deity (devadhītā). In Pali passages such as "Then a certain deity (devatā), of surpassing beauty, when the night was far spent...", the word 'deva' itself is used with a suffix in the sense of its own meaning (svāttha-taddhita) to form 'devatā', and thus a male deity is called 'devatā'. Similarly, in passages such as "Those seven hundred noble Brahmās, having departed from their mansions...", Brahmās are called 'devatā'.

"O deity (devatā), you who stand with surpassing beauty, illuminating all directions like the Osadhī star (the morning star), just as it illuminates all directions with its beautiful radiance."

In such Pali passages, a female deity is called 'devatā'.

These are the names of deities by birth (upapatti-deva):
Deva, Sura, Vibudha, Nijjara, Amara, Maru, Sudhāsī, Tidasa, Saggavāsī, Animisa, Divoka, Amatapāyī, Saggaṭṭha, and Devatāni.

The root *khi* occurs in the sense of exhaustion or destruction. *Khiyati* (is exhausted), *khaya* (destruction/cessation), *khiyana* (exhausting), *rāgakkhaya* (the destruction of lust).

The root *khi* also occurs in the senses of dwelling, anger, and harming. *Khiyati* (dwells, is angry, or harms). "Do not go to the abode of King Yama," "They are angry because of the gift of the noble elephant." In these Pali passages, *khiyati* means 'dwells'. *Yamakkhaya* means the residence of King Yama. *Khiyanti* means 'they are angry' or 'they harm'.

The root *ghā* occurs in the sense of perceiving scent. Because of the meaning *ghāyati* (smells), it is called *ghāna* (nose). To smell a scent with the nose; having smelled.

The root *ruca* occurs in the sense of delighting. *Rocana*, *ruci* (delight). "I delight in rice," "That sick person does not delight even in rice," "I delight in monkhood." To delight; having delighted. However, some teachers read the root *ruca* in this *divādi* group as having the sense of "beauty/splendor". That reading is not appropriate in any context.
223:
This is because in the root *ruca* which expresses the sense of beauty (splendor), the form "*ruccati*" does not exist. Therefore, it should be noted as follows: the root *ruca* expressing both beauty and delight belongs to the *bhūvādi* group. In that root, only forms such as "*rocati*", "*virocati*", and "*ekattamuparoicitaṃ*" (delighting in solitude) occur, not the form "*ruccati*". However, the root *ruca* expressing only delight belongs to both the *divādi* group and the *curādi* group. When it belongs to the *divādi* group, the form is "*gamanaṃ mayhaṃ ruccati*" (going is pleasing to me). When it belongs to the *curādi* group, the form is "*kiṃ nu jātiṃ na rocesi*" (why do you not delight in rebirth?). If preceded by the prefix *ā-*, it occurs in the sense of informing, and forms like "*āroceti*" and "*ārocayati*" are seen.

The root *muca* occurs in the sense of liberation. *Muccati* (is released from suffering). *Adhimuccati* (is resolved/convinced through faith). *Mutti*, *vimutti*, *adhimutti* (liberation, resolve), *muccamāna* (being released).

The root *uca* occurs in the sense of gathering or association. *Uccati* (gathers). *Oka*, *ūkā*, *ukkā*.

*Oka* refers to water or a dwelling/house. This usage of the word *oka* is found in passages such as "with robes filled with water" and "like a fish taken from its watery home (oka) and thrown onto dry land". *Ūkā* is a specific kind of insect, a louse, that arises on the head.

*Ukkā* refers to torches and so on. In the context of the passage "when torches are being held", a torch is called "*ukkā*". In the context of the passage "one should bind a fire-brand (ukkā), having bound the fire-brand, one should smear the mouth of the furnace", it refers to a fire-brand or furnace. In the context of the passage "like the bellows of smiths, it burns within and not without", it refers to the nozzle of a smith's bellows. In the context of the passage "there will be such a falling of a meteor (ukkāpāta) with such a result", the flame caused by the force of wind is called "*ukkā*". With tongs...
224:
In the context of the passage "taking gold with tongs and placing it in the mouth of the crucible (ukkāmukha)", *ukkā* should be understood as the crucible of goldsmiths. Thus:

In these five instances—torches, the flame of a meteor/wind-force, the nozzle of a smith's bellows, a crucible, and a fire-brand/furnace—the word "*ukkā*" occurs.

The root *che* occurs in the sense of cutting. *Chiyati*, *chiyanti* (cuts). *Avacchitaṃ*, *avacchātaṃ* (cut off). Having cut the topknot perfumed with excellent scent.

The root *saja* occurs in the sense of clinging. Clinging is called "*saṅga*". *Sajjati* (clings). *Sajjana*, *sajjito*, and *satto* (being/creature) are formed.

The root *yuja* occurs in the sense of right application (samādhi). Right application is called "*samādhi*". It means non-distraction by virtue of the right exertion of bodily actions and so on. *Yujjati* (is joined/yoked). *Yogo* (effort/exertion) and *yogī* (one yoked to meditation) are formed.

In this context, "*yoga*" means energy (vīriya). Indeed, because of the statement: "A wise man should surely strive, he should not be weary. I see myself as I desired to be (attaining the father's heritage)," it is called *yoga* because it is appropriate (*yujjati*) to be done without fail.

The root *ranja* occurs in the sense of staining or lust (rāga). *Rajjati* (is stained/attached), *virajjati* (is detached). *Rajjamāno*, *rajjaṃ*, *rajjanto*, *rāgo*, *virāgo*, *rajjanaṃ*, *virajjanaṃ*, and *rajanīyaṃ* are formed. By the power of prefixes (upasagga), other meanings also occur, such as the sense of "departing from one's own country" (*nirajjati*).

Among those terms, "*virāga*" means that the defiling unwholesome states are removed (*virajjanti*) in this state; therefore, it is called *virāga*. It refers to Nibbāna and the Path (magga).

The root *viji* occurs in the senses of fear and trembling. *Vijjati*, *saṃvijjati* (is terrified/trembles). *Saṃvego*, *saṃvejanīyaṃ*, *ubbijjati* (is terrified), *ubbego*, and *ubbiggahadayo* (one with a terrified heart) are formed.
225:
The root luja is used in the sense of destruction (vināsa). Because it is prone to destruction, it is called the world (loka). Lopa, lutti, lujjanna, and lutta are terms meaning destruction or deletion.

The root ṭhā is used in the sense of stopping from going (standing/remaining). Ṭhāyati—he stands. Ṭhāyī, ṭhiti, ṭhāna, ṭhita, tatraṭṭha (standing therein), tiṭṭha, kappaṭṭhāyī (one who remains for an aeon), and āsabhaṭṭhānaṭṭhāyī (one who stands in a noble position) are derived from it.

There is a scriptural example: 
“I sleep happily, I stand happily, 
I live my life happily. 
I have escaped from the hands of Māra; 
Oh, how wonderful is the Teacher’s compassion!” 
Another example is: “The quail standing in its own feeding ground.” In that passage, ṭhāyāmi means tiṭṭhāmi (I stand).

The root ḍi is used in the sense of going (flying). Ḍiyati, ḍemāno, and ḍino are terms meaning flying. The example is: “O bird flying high in the sky, with wings as your vehicle, traveler of the air... tell my wife with beautiful thighs.” Here, because of the meaning ḍiyati (he flies), the derivation ḍemāno should be taken.

The root tā is used in the sense of protecting (pālana). Tāyati—he protects. Tātā—one who protects from suffering. “That lonely father Vessantara will long lament in the hermitage.” Tāṇa, paritta, and gotta are terms meaning protection. There is a scriptural passage: “Lay follower, you have done good deeds, you have merit that protects from fear at the time of death.”

Among those terms, paritta is so called because it protects (tāyati) beings from all sides (samantato) against fear, calamity, and misfortune due to its great power. Gotta is so called because it protects knowledge (gaṃ).

The root nata is used in the sense of bending the body (dancing). Bending the body is called gatta-vināma or gatta-vikkhepa. Naccati—he dances. Nacca—dancing. Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta, the son of a stage-performer.

The root dā is used in the sense of cleaning or purifying (sodhana). Dāyati—he cleanses. Dāna—cleansing. For the purpose of causing investigation to be purified (anuyoga-dāpanattha). Having purified the investigation (anuyogaṃ datvā). Having purified the volition of giving (dāna) from the stains of stinginess, etc. (dānaṃ datvā).
226:
The root dā is used in the sense of sleeping (supana). Dāyati—he sleeps. Niddāyati—he falls asleep. Niddāyana, niddāyamāna, and niddāyanta are terms meaning sleeping.

The root dā is used in the sense of giving (dāna). A man gives (dāyati) a gift. With the prefix ā-, the root dā is used in the sense of taking (gahana). He takes (ādiyati) what is not given. He undertakes (samādiyati) the precepts. In the passive voice: A gift is given (dīyati) by the man; what is not given is taken (ādiyati). In the causative: He causes to take (ādāpeti), he causes to undertake (samādāpeti). There is a scriptural passage: “Those virtuous ones who cause only the Dhamma to be undertaken.”

The root dā is used in the sense of cutting or dividing (avakhaṇḍana). Diyati, diyanti—it cuts. Paritta—small (or sense-sphere phenomena).

In this context, paritta is so called because it is limited (khaṇḍita) from all sides. A small amount of cow dung is called paritta. Therefore, the name paritta refers to something small. Sense-sphere phenomena (kāmāvacara-dhamma) are also called paritta because of their limited power.

The root dā is used in the sense of purity (suddhi). Dāyati, vodāyati—it is pure. Vodāna—purity. This root is intransitive. Thus, it is stated in the Netti-aṭṭhakathā regarding Samatha and Vipassanā: “One is purified by this, or this itself is pure, therefore it is called vodāna.”

The root dī is used in the sense of wasting away or exhaustion (khaya). Dīyate—it wastes away. Dīna and ādīnava (danger/fault) are derived from it.

Among those terms, dīna refers to one who has reached suffering due to the exhaustion of kin, wealth, etc. Ādīnava is so called because one reaches suffering through this fault (dosa).

The root du is used in the sense of intense burning or agony (paritāpa). Duyate—he suffers agony. Duna and dūta (messenger) are derived from it.

The root bhidi is used in the sense of breaking or destruction (bhijjana). A thing of a nature to break, breaks (bhijjati). Because it is prone to breaking, it is called bhinna. Bhijjana and bheda are terms meaning destruction.

The root chidi is used in the sense of cutting or severing (chijjana). The thread breaks (chijjati). Because it is prone to breaking, it is called chinna. Likewise, chidda (a hole). Chijjana and cheda are terms meaning severing.
227:
The root khidi is used in the sense of suffering or misery (dīniya). The state of being miserable is dīniya, as in the word dakkhiya. Khijjati (he is weary/suffering), khinna, akhinnamati (the Lord who possesses a mind of great compassion free from weariness), kheda, and khedangato loko-hitāya nātho (the Lord who reached weariness for the benefit of the world).

Here, khedangato means having reached the fatigue known as physical suffering, or experiencing suffering.

The root pada is used in the sense of going (gati). Pajjati (he goes). Maggaṃ paṭipajjati (he enters the path). Paṭipattiṃ paṭipajjati (he practices the practice). Addhānamaggappaṭipanno hoti (he is one who has entered a long journey). Phalasamāpattiṃ samāpajjati (he attains the attainment of fruition). Āpattiṃ āpajjati (he falls into an offense). There is also an intransitive usage: “Unrighteousness occurs to them” (tesaṃ adhammo āpajjati). Pajjo (path), Vyagghapajjo (path), and sampadāyo (one who makes the Dhamma known).

In this context, pajjo means path (magga). Vyagghapajjo is so called because it refers to a city founded on a tiger’s path (saddūlapatha), and thus a clansman (a Koliyan prince) of that name. Sampadāyo means one by whom the Dhamma is made known; it refers to an expounder (akkhātā).

The root vida is used in the sense of existence or presence (sattā). The mode of being present is sattā. Vijjati (it exists/is known), saṃvijjati. Jātavedo (fire), vijjā (knowledge), avijjā (ignorance), and vidito (known).

Among those terms, jātavedo means fire. This is because as soon as it is born (arisen), it is known (vedayati) or recognized by the rising of clouds of smoke; therefore, it is called jātavedo. Vijjā is so called because it makes the nature of phenomena known (vidita); it refers to wisdom (ñāṇa). Avijjā is so called because it makes unknown the meaning of the aggregates as a mass (rāsaṭṭha), the meaning of the bases as spheres (āyatanaṭṭha), the meaning of the elements as empty (suññaṭṭha), the meaning of the truths as reality (tathaṭṭha), and the meaning of the faculties as predominance (adhipatiyaṭṭha). It is called avijjā because it makes unknown the fourfold meaning of suffering, etc., in terms of oppression and so on; it refers to delusion (moha).

The root mada is used in the sense of madness or intoxication (ummāda). Ummāda is defined as confusion, loss of mindfulness, or mental distraction. Majjati (he is intoxicated/negligent), pamajjati. Matto (intoxicated), surāmadamatto (intoxicated by the madness of liquor). “O Great King, being intoxicated, I ate the flesh of my son.” Mattahatthī (an elephant in rut), pamatto (a negligent person), and ummatto (a mad person).
228:
Heedfulness (appamāda) is the path to the Deathless; heedlessness (pamāda) is the path to death. Those who are heedful do not die; those who are heedless are as if already dead.

The root mid- is used in the sense of affection (sinehana). There are terms such as mejjati (he loves), mettā, metti (loving-kindness), mittaṃ (friend), and mitto (companion).

The root antaradhā- is used in the sense of disappearance (adassana). The root dhā- preceded by the word antara- occurs in the sense of the disappearance of an existing object. There are terms such as antaradhāyati (it disappears), antaradhānaṃ (disappearance), and antaradhāyanto (one who is disappearing). "That deity vanished (antarahitā)." "It also disappears in between (antarāpidhāyati)."

The root budh- is used in the sense of understanding (avagamana). Understanding means knowing (jānana). There are terms such as bujjhati (he knows), buddhā (Buddha), buddhi (wisdom), buddhaṃ (knowledge), bodho (enlightenment), and bodhi (enlightenment). "He has known the Truths (bujjhitā)." "He has known all (buddhā)." "One who has known (buddhavā)." "He causes to know (vibodheti)." "One who causes to know (bodhetā)." "One who is awakened (buddhā)." "One who is blossomed (vibuddhā)," and so forth.

Among those terms, "Buddha" is so called because He has known the Four Noble Truths; He is called "Buddha" because He awakens the multitude of beings. Alternatively, He is called "Buddha" because He has known all that is knowable (ñeyya) through wisdom perfected by the perfections (pāramīs). Some teachers, however, desiring the word "Buddha" to be established as a passive derivative (kammasādhana), define it thus: "'That Blessed One is indeed the Sammāsambuddha,' thus He is called 'Buddha' because He is to be known by the Arahants who have attained special qualities and have destroyed the taints." The detailed explanation should be taken according to the method stated in the Niddesa. "Buddhi" is so called because one knows by it. In this same way, buddhaṃ, bodho, and bodhi are formed. Alternatively, the act of knowing is called "buddhi." In this same way, bodho and bodhi are formed. All these terms are synonyms for wisdom (paññā).

Now, I shall set forth the various meanings of the word "bodhi." The word "bodhi" refers to the tree, the Path, omniscience, Nibbāna, and also a person of that name. For instance, in passages such as "First awakened at the foot of the Bodhi tree," and "Between the Bodhi and Gayā," the word "bodhi" refers to the tree. In the phrase "In the four paths...
229:
...knowledge," the word refers to the Path. In the passage, "The Great Wise One of noble wisdom reached Bodhi," it refers to omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa). In the passage, "Having reached Bodhi, the deathless, the unconditioned," it refers to Nibbāna. In passages such as, "Venerable Sir, Prince Bodhi pays homage to the feet of the Blessed One with his head," and "A noble disciple is called Bodhi," it refers to a person designated by that name.

On this, it is said:
The word "Bodhi" occurs in the sense of the tree, the Path, Nibbāna, knowledge, omniscience, and likewise in designation.

Because one knows, one is a "bujjhitā"; because one causes others to know, one is a "bodhetā."

In this context, I shall show some usages and forms such as the infinitive (tumanta). "The person who makes known the hidden meaning that was not understood (asambuddhaṃ) by others deserves to make others understand (sambuddhuṃ)." The forms are bujjhituṃ, buddhuṃ (to know), bujjhitvā, bujjhitvāna, bujjhituna, buddhiya, buddhiyāna, buddhā, buddhāna (having known).

Among those, "asambuddha" means a meaning not known by others; there is also a variant reading "asambodha," meaning a meaning that is not proper to make others know. "Sambuddhuṃ" means to know (saṃbujjhituṃ). "Buddhā" means having known (bujjhityā); the same applies to the word "buddhāna."

Some teachers, however, say: "In the Nāmarūpapariccheda, because we find the word 'budhvā' with the conjunct of 'dh' and 'v' in phrases like 'having known by the Bodhi-path (bodhimaggena budhvā)' and 'the Sugata, having known at the foot of the Bodhi tree (budhvā bodhitale),' and because it ends with the suffix -tvā, the word 'budhvā' should be accepted as established through the conjunct of 'dh' and 'v'." They say this because such a word-form is not seen in the Buddha's words (Pali Canon), and because it is inconsistent with the Buddha's words, and in pure...
230:
...ancient manuscripts, the word is seen as "bodhimaggena buddhā" and "buddhā bodhitale," devoid of the 'v' conjunct; therefore, the form 'budhvā' should not be accepted. Indeed, such a reading is not consistent with the Buddha's words. Even if one were to search the Buddha's words for a hundred or a thousand years, one would not find such a word with the 'v' and 'dh' conjunct. Thus, the word-form "budhvā" should be understood as inconsistent with the Buddha's words. That form is desired only by scholars who have been deceived by their familiarity with Sanskrit (Sakkaṭa) texts, not by those who know the Saddanīti. Here, these illustrative examples should be understood:

"Who, having struck (viddhā) me, remains hidden?"
"A mortal, if he obtains (laddhā) what he desires (is happy)."
"Having known (laddhāna) the distinction between what comes before and after, one may go to where the King of Death sees not."
"Having seen (diṭṭhā) Ummādantī wearing jeweled earrings,
I cannot sleep day or night, like one who has lost a thousand."

In those verses, "viddhā" means having struck. "Laddhā" means having obtained. "Laddhāna" means having obtained. "Diṭṭhā" means having seen. Thus, although the words "viddhā, laddhā, laddhāna, diṭṭhā" occur with the -tvā suffix, they do not have a connection with the letter 'v' through a conjunct. Therefore, these words "buddhā, buddhāna" should also be taken as forms devoid of the 'v' conjunct, just like "laddhā, laddhāna," etc. Those who desire and recite the form "budhvā," I think they are deceived by the -tvā suffix; because of that deception, they fall into error. Therefore, without accepting such a form, the venerable ones should believe in the word-analysis (saddavinicchaya) stated in the Saddanīti as the essence.

The root budh- is used in the sense of understanding (bodhana). This root is both transitive and intransitive. This is because by the utterance of the word "bodhana," knowing, blossoming, and the end of sleep (awakening) are encompassed. Therefore, it is said: "budh in the sense of knowledge (ñāṇa), budh in the sense of blossoming (vikasana), budh in the sense of the end of sleep (niddakkhaya)." The Blessed One knows (bujjhati); He knows the dhammas (bujjhati); He awakens (pabujjhati). The lotus blossoms (bujjhati). The man is awake (buddhā, pabuddhā); he knows or he wakes up (bodhati, pabodhati), and so forth.
231:
The root Saṃdhā is used in the sense of joining (sandhi). The root dhā with the prefix saṃ- has the function of joining. In the sentence, "For that King Vessantara, Queen Maddī has no frown, nor is she joined with mental distress (not depressed), nor does she weep," the form 'na sandhiyati' is a Divādi class form that is not common to other treatises.

The root Dhanu is used in the sense of longing or craving (yācana). In the sentence, "Dear daughter Irandatī, your mother longs for the heart of the minister Vidhura," the form 'dhaniyyati' is also a Divādi class form not common to other treatises.

The root Dhī is used in the sense of disrespect (anādara). There are forms such as dhīyate and dhīno.

The root Yudha is used in the sense of striking or fighting (sampahāra). There are forms such as yujjhati, yodho (warrior), yuddhaṃ (battle), and caraṇāyudho (a cock, having weapons in its feet). By changing the letter 'y' to 'v', the form 'āvudha' (weapon) is produced. Therein, caraṇāyudho refers to a cock.

The root Kudha is used in the sense of anger (kopa). There are forms such as kujjhati, kodho, kujjhanā, and kujjhitattaṃ. It is said: "An angry person does not know the benefit; an angry person does not see the Dhamma."

The root Sudha is used in the sense of purity (soceyya). Soceyya means the state of being pure. There are forms such as sujjhati, suddhi, visuddhi, sujjhanaṃ, suddhā, visuddhā, and parisuddhā. In the causative, there are sodheti (purifies), sodhako (one who purifies), and so forth.

The root Sidhu is used in the sense of accomplishment (saṃrādhana). There are forms such as sijjhati and siddhi.

The root Radha is used in the sense of harming (hiṃsā). There are forms such as rajjhati, virajjhati (to fail/err), aparajjhati (to offend), and aparādho (offense).

The roots Rādha and Sādha are used in the sense of complete accomplishment (saṃsiddhi). There are forms such as rādhayati, sādhayati, ārādhanaṃ, and sādhanaṃ. A virtuous person is called 'sādhu' because they accomplish the benefit of themselves and others. Excellent deeds such as giving (dāna) and virtue (sīla) that are obtained because they are greatly accomplished are called 'sādhu'.

The root Vidha is used in the sense of piercing (vijjhana). There are forms such as vijjhati and paṭivijjhati. There are also forms such as khaṇa (dig!), viddha (pierce!), vidhu (one who pierces), vijjhanako, viddhā, paṭividdhā, vijjhanaṃ, vedho, paṭivedho, vijjhitvā, viddhā, and viddhāna. It is said: "Who pierced me and is hiding?"

The root Idha is used in the sense of prosperity (vuddhi). There are forms such as ijjhati, samijjhati, iddhi, ijjhanaṃ, samijjhanaṃ, and iddhā. Therein, iddhi means accomplishment. Alternatively, it is called iddhi because beings accomplish through this power, and they reach prosperity, abundance, and excellence.
232:
The root Gidhu is used in the sense of intense desire (abhikaṅkhā). There are forms such as gijjhati (to long for) and gijjho (vulture). Gaddhā is also a vulture. "Gaddhabādhipubbo" refers to the monk Ariṭṭha, who was formerly born in a vulture-killing clan. There is also the Pali: "Kāmagiddhā na jānāsi," meaning "You, King Vedeha, obsessed with sensual pleasures, do not know [the danger of death]." Gedho means attachment.

The root Rudhi is used in the sense of obstruction (āvaraṇa). There are forms such as rujjhati (obstructs), virujjhati (opposes), and paṭivirujjhati (repeatedly opposes). Virodhako is one who opposes, and viruddhā is one who is opposed. Rodho, virodho, paṭivirodho, and anuvirodho are in the senses of opposition and repeated opposition.

Anuvidhā consists of the root dhā with the prefixes anu and vi, used in the sense of imitating others (anukaraṇa). The root dhā with the prefix anuvipubba- functions in the sense of following an action (imitation). A man imitates the actions of another man. In this regard, there is this Pali: "The auspicious state horse of the King of Bārāṇasī named Sāma, being corrupted by the horse-trainer named Giridatta through his limping and crooked gait, abandoned his former natural, graceful, and majestic gait, and went about imitating only that limping and crooked gait of the trainer Giridatta." This is also an uncommon Divādi class form.

Anurudha is used in the sense of desire (kāma). Kāma means desire (icchā). The root rudha with the prefix anu- functions in the sense of desiring. There are forms such as anuruddhā and anurodho. There is also the usage "Anusmāti kiṃ virodho." Therein, anuruddhā is so called because one desires (anurujjhati) very excellent objects. Anurodho means compliance (anukūlatā). This Pali is: "He is intensely attached to gain that has arisen, and is opposed to loss."

Vyadha is used in the sense of striking (tāḷana). There is the form vyajjhati. Vyādho means a hunter (luddho). He is called vyādho because he harms and kills various animals.

Gudha is used in the sense of enveloping (pariveṭhana). There is the form gujjhati. Godhā is a monitor lizard.

Mana is used in the sense of knowing (ñāṇa). There are forms such as maññati (knows), avamaññati (knows as inferior/despises), and atimaññati (excessively disdains). It is called māno (pride) because one perceives oneself as superior, etc. Synonyms include maññanā (conceiving), maññitattaṃ (the fault of conceiving), māno (pride), ahaṅkāro (egoism), unnati (loftiness), ketu (banner-like), paggaho (exaltation), and avalepo (smearing with pride).
233:
The root *jan* is in the sense of generating (*janana*). This root is transitive (*sakammaka*). The form '*jaññati*' means 'does' or 'accomplishes'. In the causative form (*kārita*), it is found as: "Mother Phussatī generated (gave birth to) me." It is used in expressions such as '*janayati*', '*sukhaṃ janeti*' (generates happiness), and so on. Because of the sense '*janayati*' (one who generates), it is called '*janaka*' (father), or it can refer to anyone who generates. Because one generates defilements in various ways, one is called a worldling (*puthujjana*). Among those forms, '*janeti*' and '*janayati*' become simple active forms (*suddha-kattu*) when they belong to the *curādi* group. The meaning of those simple active forms is 'does'. By the power of the causative (*hetu-kattu*), the meaning of that word is also said to be 'causes to arise' (*nibbatteti*).

The root *janī* is in the sense of manifestation (*pātubhāva*). This root ends in '-ī' and is intransitive (*akammaka*). However, if the prefix '*vi-*' is present, it becomes transitive. A son is born (*jāyati*); he is one who has been born (*jāta*). In this being, defilements arise in various ways; therefore, he is called a worldling (*puthujjana*). '*Janana*' (arising) is called birth (*jāti*). '*Sañjāti*', '*nibbatti*', '*abhinibbatti*', and the manifestation of the aggregates are synonyms of '*jāti*'. A woman gives birth to a son; a woman is one who has given birth to a son. That unpleasant man causes unhappiness even to the mother who gave birth to him. A woman who is about to give birth is called '*upavijaññā*'. In the causative form, there are forms such as '*jāpeti*' and '*jāpayati*'. It is said, "Wisdom that causes benefit to arise is called '*atthajāpikā paññā*'."

The root *han* is in the sense of harming (*hiṃsā*). Here, by the word 'harming', 'striking' or 'impinging' (*ghaṭṭana*) should be understood. Sound strikes the ear (*haññati*), it impinges (*paṭihaññati*). The voice of the Blessed One impinges on the worldly ear. These are active voice words (*kattu-pada*). When belonging to the *bhūvādi* group, in the Pali "Gold is indeed struck by iron, they do not strike iron with gold," the word '*haññati*' is a passive voice word (*kamma-pada*). It means gold is struck by smiths with iron. The word '*hananti*' is an active voice word (*kattu-pada*). It means smiths strike iron with gold. Here, '*hanana*' should be understood as striking (*paharaṇa*).

The root *rup* is in the sense of being affected or deformed (*ruppana*). Being affected means being disturbed (*kuppana*), impinged upon (*ghaṭṭana*), or oppressed (*pīḷana*). It is affected (*ruppati*). Form (*rūpaṃ*), being affected (*ruppanaṃ*). If this root *rup* in the *curādi* group is in the sense of 'the act of showing form' (*rūpa-kriyā*), the forms '*rūpeti*' and '*rūpayati*' occur.
234:
Among those things, why is 'form' (*rūpa*) called 'form'? It is called 'form' because of the sense of being affected (*ruppana*). This was spoken by the Blessed One as follows: "Monks, why is it called 'form'? Monks, it is called 'form' because it is affected (*ruppati*). By what is it affected? It is affected by cold, it is affected by heat, it is affected by hunger, it is affected by thirst, and it is affected by the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things. Monks, it is called 'form' because it is affected."

In that statement, 'is affected' (*ruppati*) means it is disturbed, it is impinged upon, it is oppressed, it is broken. 'It is broken' means it undergoes change/deformation. Undergoing change means the arising of a form dissimilar to the previous state when encountering opposing conditions such as cold and so on. Here, by the word 'is disturbed (*kuppati*)', the derivation of the word '*rūpa*' in the active sense (*kattu*) is shown. By the words 'is impinged upon (*ghaṭṭiyati*)' and 'is oppressed (*pīḷiyati*)', the derivation of the word '*rūpa*' in the passive sense (*kamma*) is shown. For the action such as being disturbed (*kuppana*) is indeed the action of being affected (*ruppana*). To show that this meaning, whether active or passive, is simply 'being broken', it is said: "The meaning is 'it is broken' (*bhijjati*)."

Alternatively, the derivation of the word '*rūpa*' is stated in the reflexive/middle sense (*kamma-kattu*) as "it is called form because it is affected." Because deformation itself is called '*ruppana*'. Therefore, the meaning is shown by the word '*bhijjati*' which has a reflexive sense of 'it breaks'. In that context, when the word '*ruppati*' is in the passive sense, words like '*sītena*' (by cold) are in the instrumental case (*karaṇa-vacana*) with an agentive meaning (*kattu*). But when the word '*ruppati*' is in the active or reflexive sense, words like '*sītena*' should be understood as the instrumental case in the sense of cause (*hetu*).

The word '*rūpa*' occurs in the senses of aggregate (*khandha*), existence (*bhava*), sign (*nimitta*), cause (*paccaya*), body (*sarīra*), color (*vaṇṇa*), shape (*saṇṭhāna*), and so on. This word '*rūpa*' occurs in the sense of the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) in the phrase: "Whatever form there is, past, future, or present." It occurs in the sense of fine-material existence (*rūpa-bhava*) in the phrase: "He develops the path (jhāna) for the sake of rebirth in the fine-material realm." In the phrase: "Perceiving no form internally, [he sees] external [forms]..."
235:
...he sees [external forms]"—in this phrase, it occurs in the sense of the *kasiṇa* sign (*nimitta*). In the phrase: "Monks, evil unwholesome states arise with a cause (*sarūpā*), not without a cause"—it occurs in the sense of cause (*paccaya*). In the phrase: "The space enclosed by bones and flesh comes to be known as 'form' (*rūpa*)"—it occurs in the sense of the body (*sarīra*). In the phrase: "Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises"—it occurs in the sense of color/visible object (*vaṇṇa*). In the phrase: "He takes the physical form as a measure; he has confidence in the physical form"—it occurs in the sense of shape/appearance (*saṇṭhāna*). Thus:

The word '*rūpa*' occurs in the sense of aggregate, existence, sign, body, cause, color, shape, and so on.

The root *kup* is in the sense of anger. *Kuppati*—he is angry. They are even angry at the wind that blows. *Kopa*, *pakopa*—anger. "One should guard against verbal anger (*vacī-pakopa*)."

The root *tap* is in the sense of burning/distress (*santāpa*). *Tappati*, *santappati*—he is distressed. *Santāpa*—distress/heat.
The root *tap* is in the sense of satisfaction (*pīṇana*). *Tappati*—he is satisfied. *Tappanaṃ*—satisfaction.

The root *dap* is in the sense of joy (*hāsa*). *Dappati*—he is joyful.

The root *dīp* is in the sense of illumination (*ditti*). *Dippati*—it shines. *Dīpa*—island, lamp.

The root *lup* is in the sense of invisibility/elision (*adassana*). *Luppanaṃ*, *lopa*, *lutti*—elision, disappearance.

The root *khip* is in the sense of sending/speed (*pēraṇa*). *Khippati*—it is fast. *Khippaṃ*—quickly.

The root *lubh* is in the sense of greed/clinging (*giddhi*). *Lubbhati*—he is greedy/clings. "He stands leaning (*olubbha*) on his own knee." *Lubbhanaṃ*, *lobha*—greed. *Lubbhitvā*, *lubbhitvāna*, *lubbhiya*, *lubbhiyāna*—having clung. *Olubbhitvā*, *olubbhitvāna*, *olubbhiya*, *olubbhiyāna*—having leaned. *Lubbhitum*, *olubbhitum*—to cling, to lean.

Among those, 'greed' (*lobha*) means that by which beings are greedy, or it is greedy itself, or it is just the state of being greedy; therefore it is called '*lobha*'. Here, "Greed...
236:
Lubbhana, lubbhitatta, rāga, taṇhā, tasiṇā, mucchā, ejā, vana, vanatha, and so forth, should be known as the many names of greed (lobha).

The root khubha is used in the sense of agitation (sañcalana). It takes the forms khubbati and saṅkhubbati. The city of Cetuttara is agitated (khubbittha). Saṅkhobha means agitation. In the causative (kārita), it is khobheti and khobhayati.

The root samu is used in the sense of calming (upasama). The mind is calmed, specifically calmed, or thoroughly calmed (sammati, upasammati, vūpasammati). There are terms such as samaṇa (ascetic), santi (peace), and santa (one who is peaceful).

In this context, a samaṇa is so called because he has a calmed mind (samitacitta). According to the causative sense, the definition (nibbacana) should be understood as one who calms (sameti, upasameti) the defilements. Therefore, two causative forms are found: "That which calms [the heat of defilements], this is noble" and "He calms the [heat of] beings in this world."

The root samu is also used in the sense of exhaustion (kheda) and cessation (nirodha). Exhaustion is called kheda. Reaching the state of non-existence is called nirodha. The body of one who has traveled a long distance is exhausted (sammati). Fire is extinguished (sammati). There is the term santa.

The word santa occurs in the sense of exhaustion in sentences such as "A league is long to the weary (santa)." It occurs in the sense of cessation in sentences such as "This thought (vitakka) and this evaluation (vicāra) have ceased (santā), have been calmed." It occurs in the sense of being the object of subtle knowledge in sentences such as "This Dhamma I have attained is profound, hard to see, hard to understand, peaceful (santa), and sublime." It occurs in the sense of the calming of defilements in sentences such as "For one who is calmed (upasanta), always mindful." It occurs in the sense of the virtuous in sentences such as "The virtuous (santo) indeed make [the Dhamma] known with the virtuous." It occurs in the sense of existence in sentences such as "Monks, these five great thieves exist (santo), are found." In this regard, it is said:
237:
“In the sense of being weary, in the sense of having ceased, in the sense of being the object of subtle wisdom, in the calming of defilements, in the sense of existence, and in the sense of the virtuous—in these six instances, the word santa is found.”

The root damu is used in the sense of taming (damana). Dammati—he tames. Danto—tamed/disciplined, damo—taming, damanaṃ—taming. In the causative (kārita), the forms are “he tames the mind” (cittaṃ dameti, damayati).

Therein, damo is a name for the restraint of the sense faculties (indriyasaṃvara) and so forth. In the passage, “Tamed by truth, endowed with restraint (damasā), one who has reached the end of the Vedas, who has lived the holy life,” the restraint of the sense faculties is called dama. In the passage, “If truth, restraint (dama), generosity, and patience are found to be greater in this world,” wisdom (paññā) is called dama. In the passage, “By giving, by restraint (damena), by self-control, and by truthful speech,” the practice of the Uposatha is called dama. In the passage, “By patience and calming (damūpasamena),” patience (khanti) is called dama. Thus:

“Restraint of the sense faculties, wisdom, patience, and also the Uposatha—these meanings are expressed by the word dama in the Dispensation (Sāsana).”

The root yā is used in the sense of going (gati) and reaching (pāpuṇa). Yāyati—he goes, yāyanti—they go. Pariyāyo—method/discourse. The Great King, traveling in the Vejayanta chariot, saw the mountains between the seven Sīdā oceans. Yāyanto—one who is going. He follows after the one who is going. Yātānuyāyī—one who follows and performs a favor previously done. Yāyituṃ, yāyitvā, and so forth, are formed.

Here, the extraction of the meanings of the word pariyāya will be stated. The word pariyāya is used in the sense of turn (vāra), teaching (desanā), cause (kāraṇa), a place to be reached from all sides (samantato gantabbaṭṭhāna), and similarity (sadisa). In sentences such as “Ānanda, whose turn (pariyāyo) is it today to exhort the bhikkhunīs?”, it is used in the sense of turn. In sentences such as “Remember this as the Honeyball Discourse (madhupiṇḍikapariyāya)”, it is used in the sense of teaching. In sentences such as “By this reason (pariyāyena), Prince, it is thus...”
238:
“...let it be,” and so forth, it is used in the sense of cause. In “pariyāyapatho” (a path to be traversed), it is used in the sense of a place to be reached from all sides. In “the word kopa is similar (pariyāya) to the word khobha,” it is used in the sense of similarity. Thus:

“The word pariyāya may be used in the sense of turn, teaching, cause, a place to be reached from all sides, and similarity.”

The root ri is used in the sense of dwelling (vasana). Riyati—he dwells.

The root vilī is used in the sense of melting (vilīnabhāva). Ghee melts (vilīyati). In the causative, vilāpayati—he causes to melt.

The root vā is used in the sense of going (gati) and smelling (gandhana). Vāyati—it blows/goes, it smells. Vāyo, vāto—wind.

The root sivu is used in the sense of stretching threads (tantasantāna). Sibbati, saṃsibbati—he sews/joins. Sibbaṃ, sibbanto. In the causative, sibbeti, sibbayati, sibbāpeti, sibbāpayati—he causes to sew.

The root sivu is also used in the sense of going (gati) and drying (sosana). Sibbati—he goes, he dries.

The roots dhivu and khivu are used in the sense of pointing out (nidassana). Dhibbati, khibbati—he points out.

The root sā is used in the sense of making thin (tanukaraṇa). Siyati, siyanti—he makes thin.

The root sā is used in the sense of making an end (antakamma). Because it makes an end of (cuts off) conceit without remainder, the Path of Arahantship is called mānasantī.

The root sā is used in the sense of tasting (assādana). He tastes (licks) the flavor. Sāyitaṃ, sāyanaṃ.

The root si is used in the sense of livelihood (pāṇippasava) and giving birth. Sūyati—he lives/makes a living, pasūyati—she gives birth. A cow that has given birth (pasūtā gāvī).

The root kusu is used in the sense of carrying (haraṇa) and shining (ditti). Kusayati—he carries, he shines.

The root silisa is used in the sense of embracing (āliṅgana). Silissati—he embraces. Sileso—resin/adhesive.

The root kilisa is used in the sense of afflicting (upatāpa). Kilissati, saṃkilissati—he is afflicted/defiled. Kileso, saṃkileso—defilement. With the elision of the vowel ‘i’, it becomes klissati.
239: In words such as kilesa, the term kilisasadda also refers to impurity; one wears soiled clothes. Because roots have various meanings, it also refers to impurity in such passages as "Beings are defiled by a defiled mind." The root masa occurs in the sense of scarcity and patience. Massati—is scarce, is patient. The root lisa occurs in the sense of reaching. Lissati—reaches. Leso—a bowl. Teachers also read it as "lisa lesane." The root tasa occurs in the sense of thirst. Tassati, paritassati—longs for, is thirsty. Paritassanā—longing, tasiṇā—craving (taṇhā), tasito—one who is thirsty. The root dusa occurs in the sense of offending. Dussati—offends. Doso—anger, dosanaṃ—offending, dosito—offended. The root dusa occurs in the sense of displeasure. Dussati, padussati—destroys, offends. Doso, padoso—offending, duṭṭho, paduṭṭho—offended, dūsako—one who destroys, dūsito—destroyed, dūsanā—destruction. The root asu occurs in the sense of throwing. Khepo means throwing. Assati—throws. Nirassati ādiyati ca dhammaṃ—he both rejects and takes up the Dhamma. Issāso—an archer. In this context, nirassati means he rejects the teacher as well as the preaching of the Dhamma and so on. Issāso is called so because he throws (assati) arrows; thus, it means an archer. The root yasu occurs in the sense of exertion. Yassati—exerts. Niyasakammaṃ—the act of subordination. In this context, by which disciplinary act a foolish monk is made to exert himself in living in dependence, saying "You must live in dependence on a teacher," and is made to approach a teacher, it is called niyasa. That act is called niyasakamma. However, in the phrase "O Yakkha, perform the niyasakamma for me," the act of punishment is called niyasakamma. The root bhassa occurs in the sense of speaking. Bhassati—speaks. Bhassaṃ—speech, bhassakārako—a speaker. The root vasa occurs in the sense of making a sound. Sakuṇo vassati—the bird chirps. "Dear, the jackal, the lowest of beasts, howls." Maṇḍūko vassati—the frog croaks.
240:
The root nasa occurs in the sense of invisibility (destruction). A thing of a nature to perish, perishes. It perishes greatly. It perishes specifically. There is also: "O low woman, go to ruin; O unloved novice, run away, go to ruin." It has perished; it has specifically perished. In the causative (kārita): nāseti, nāsayati—causes to perish, makes perish.

The root susa occurs in the sense of drying up. The leaf dries. In the causative: the wind dries the leaf, makes it dry. In the passive (kamma): the leaf is dried by the wind. In the impersonal (bhāva), the verbal form is not well-known. Soso (the disease of consumption), dry wood. Drying, one who dries. A drying pond.

The root tusa occurs in the sense of satisfaction. He is satisfied, he is greatly content and satisfied. Contentment, satisfaction, causing satisfaction, should be contented with, should be satisfied with, the Tusita deity. In the causative: "toseti", etc., occur.

The root hā occurs in the sense of decline. It declines, it declines greatly. There (when the noble steed is brought out), the she-asses decline (in speed). In the impersonal (bhāva), there are forms such as: "Whether it be fear, or trembling, or hair-standing-on-end, that will be abandoned (pahīyissati)," and "Lust is abandoned (pahīyati)." In the passive (kamma), the verbal form is not well-known. This form "rāgo pahīyati" is a form of the root belonging to the Bhūvādi group mentioned as "hā cāge" (to give up), because the active form "rāgaṃ pajahati" (he abandons lust) is found.

The root naha occurs in the sense of binding. He binds. He binds nearby. He binds specifically. Armor (sannāho). It has been bound.

The root muha occurs in the sense of delusion. He is deluded, he is greatly deluded, he is specifically deluded. Delusion, specific delusion. A deluded person. A very deluded man. A very deluded mind. In the causative: moheti—causes to be deluded (makes foolish). One who causes delusion. Here, "momūho" is called so because of the absence of clear knowledge; it means one who is greatly deluded or very foolish.

The roots saha and suha occur in the sense of capability. He is capable. He is capable.
241:
The root Nhā is in the sense of purity. There is the form nhāyati; by the increase of letters in words with few letters, there is also nahāyati. Nahāyitvā, nhāyitvā (having bathed). Nahānaṃ, nhānaṃ (bathing). Sīsaṃ nhāto (having washed the head, he bathes). Here, "sīsaṃ nhāto" should be understood as "having washed the head, he bathes," as this is the intended meaning of the ancient teachers. The root Siniha is in the sense of affection. Sinihyati (he loves/is affectionate). There are terms such as sinehako, sinehito, siniddhā. Affection arises for the son. By the elision of the letter 'i', it becomes sneho. That this is so is seen in the Pali: "I desire the absence of greed (nissneha)." The root Viriḷa is in the sense of shame and in the sense of instigating blame. Viriḷito (he is ashamed). The meaning is well-known through the power of shame, but not through the power of instigation. Therefore, teachers who explain the meaning say, "Viriḷito means ashamed (lazzito)," and they also say, "he has reached the state of being ashamed."

Divādī ettakā diṭṭhā, dhātavo me yathābalaṃ.
Suttesvaññepi pekkhitvā, gaṇhvho atthayuttito.
I have shown these roots of the Divādi-gaṇa according to my ability. Having looked for other roots in the rules (suttas) as well, you should take them according to their appropriate meaning.

## Divādigaṇoyaṃ.
## Svādigaṇika

The root Su is in the sense of hearing. There are forms such as "suṇoti, suṇāti (he hears). Suṇiṃsu (they heard). Paṭissuṇi, paṭissuṇiṃsu (he assented, they assented). Assosi, assosuṃ (he heard, they heard). Paccassosi, paccassosuṃ (he replied, they replied)," and so on, and "suṇissati, sossati (he will hear)," and so on. In the context of reduplication (abbhāsa), there are "sussūsati (he listens), sussūsā (listening)," and so on. In the context of non-reduplication: sāvako (disciple), soto (stream/ear), suṇaṃ, suṇanto, suṇamāno (hearing), suyyamāno (being heard), savanaṃ (hearing), sutaṃ (heard). Or it is called sutaṃ because of the meaning "it was heard" (asuyittha). Sutavā (one who has heard), sotaṃ (ear), soṇo (dog), suṇituṃ, sotuṃ (to hear). Suṇitvā, suṇiya, suṇiyāna, sutvā, sutvāna (having heard). In the causative (kārita): sāveti, sāvayati (he causes to hear). In the passive (kamma): the sound is heard (suyyati, sūyati). In the abstract (bhāva), the word-form is not well-known.
242: In this context, 'Sāvaka' means a disciple (antevāsika). This disciple is of two types: one who has attained the fruit (āgatapphala) and one who has not yet attained the fruit (anāgatapphala). Among these two, the one who has attained the fruit is called 'Sāvaka' because they are born into the Noble lineage at the end of hearing [the Dhamma]. The other (anāgatapphala) is called 'Sāvaka' because they listen to the advice of teachers. Sāvaka, antevāsika, and sissa are synonymous terms. Here, I shall explain the extraction of the meaning of the word 'suta' along with the extraction of the meaning of the word 'sota'. The word 'suta' exists both with a prefix and without a prefix due to the absence of a preceding word. The word 'suta' is found in the senses of: going, fame, wetness, application (exertion), and accumulation; and also in the senses of sound and things known by following the ear-door. To illustrate: in passages such as 'senāya pasuto' (he goes to the army), it has the meaning of 'one who goes'. In 'sutadhammassa passato' (for one who sees the famous Dhamma), it has the meaning of 'one who has famous Dhamma'. In 'avassutā avassutassa purisapuggalassa' (a woman wet with defilements for a man who is wet), it has the meaning of 'one who is wet'. In 'ye jhānappasutā dhīrā' (those wise ones who are devoted to Jhāna), it has the meaning of 'those who are devoted'. In 'tumhehi puññaṃ pasutaṃ anappakaṃ' (you have accumulated much merit), it has the meaning of 'accumulated'. In 'diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ mutaṃ viññātaṃ' (seen, heard, sensed, known), it has the meaning of 'sound'. In 'bahussuto hoti sutadharo sutasannicayo' (he is very learned, a retainer of what is heard, an accumulator of what is heard), it has the meaning of 'a retainer of the Dhamma known by following the ear-door'. The word 'sota' also has many different meanings. To illustrate: It is found in the senses of the physical mass (sotapasāda), consciousness, and wisdom; and also in craving and so on. It is also found in a current [of water], the Noble Path, and the mental continuity. In terms such as 'sotāyatana, sotadhātu, sotindriya', the word 'sota' refers to the ear-sensitivity (sotapasāda) located in the physical mass. In 'sotena saddaṃ sutvā' (having heard a sound with the ear-consciousness), it refers to ear-consciousness. In 'dibbāya sotadhātuyā' (with the divine ear-element/wisdom), it refers to the wisdom-ear. In 'yāni sotāni lokasmiṃ' (whatever streams there are in the world), it refers to the five things: craving, views, defilements, misconduct, and ignorance. In 'bhagavā gangāya nadiyā sotena vuyhamānaṃ... dārukkhandhaṃ' (The Blessed One saw a large log being carried along by the current of the Ganges river), it refers to the water current.
243: In terms such as 'sotāyatana, sotadhātu, sotindriya', the word 'sota' refers to the ear-sensitivity (maṃsasota) located in the physical mass. In sentences such as 'sotena saddaṃ sutvā', it refers to ear-consciousness. In sentences such as 'dibbāya sotadhātuyā', it refers to the wisdom-ear (the divine ear-faculty). In sentences such as 'whatever streams there are in the world', it refers to the five things: the stream of craving, the stream of views, the stream of defilements, the stream of misconduct, and the stream of ignorance, which have been extensively taught by the Buddha. In sentences such as 'The Blessed One saw a large log being carried along by the current of the Ganges river', it refers to the water current. In sentences such as 'Friends, this name "sota" (stream) is a designation for the Noble Eightfold Path', it refers to the Noble Path. In sentences such as 'He knows the stream of consciousness (viññāṇasota) of a person, which is uninterrupted on both sides, established in this world and established in the next world', it refers to the mental continuity. 'Soṇa' means a dog. It is called 'soṇa' because it hears (suṇāti) the master's word. Its names are as follows: sunakha, sārameyya, suṇa, sūna, kukkura, soṇa, svāna, suvāna, sāḷura, migadaṃsana, sā, and sunidhā—these words are used for male dogs. Sunakhī, kukkurī, and sī—these words are used for female dogs. Plural words such as sunakhā and sārameyyā are used for both male and female dogs. This same method applies to other words as well.
244: Among those words for dog, the word 'kukkura' originates from the 'ku-ku' sound made during puppyhood, but it is also used for adult dogs by conventional usage (rūḷhi). To illustrate this, the commentators in the Kukkura Jātaka, regarding the passage 'Those dogs (kukkura) grown in the royal palace, well-bred and endowed with beauty and strength', explained the meaning thus: 'Kukkura means dogs. For example, even fresh urine is called "putrid urine" (pūtimutta); a fox born that very day is called an "old fox" (jarasingāla); a tender elephant-creeper is called a "putrid creeper" (pūtilatā); and even a body with a golden complexion is called a "putrid body" (pūtikāya). Similarly, even a hundred-year-old dog is called "kukkura". Therefore, even though they were large-bodied and strong, those dogs were simply called "kukkura".' The root 'Ki' is used in the sense of harming (hiṃsā). The forms are: kiṇoti, kiṇāti, kiṇanti. The root 'Sak' is used in the sense of ability (sāmatthiya). Ability is called 'sāmatthiya', like the word 'dakkhiya'. The forms are: sakkuṇāti, sakkuṇanti, asakkhi, sakkhissati, sakko, sakkī. In this context, 'Sakka' refers to the King of Devas (Sakra). He is called 'Sakka' because he is able (sakkuṇāti) to perform the welfare of others and his own welfare. Furthermore, anyone born into the Sakyan clan is also called 'Sakka'. Thus, it is said: 'At that time, Mahānāma the Sakyan...' and so on. The hermit Pingiya also addressed the Blessed One: 'O Sakka (Sakyan), deliver me from the suffering of saṃsāra.' Based on the statement, 'Friends, these princes are indeed able to protect their clan; friends, these princes are indeed very capable,' all those born in the Sakyan clan are called 'Sakya', 'Sākiya', and 'Sakka'. In this root 'Sak', although it belongs to the Svādi group, because it is a polysyllabic root (anekassara), only the 'uṇā' suffix occurs; it should be noted that the 'ṇu' and 'ṇā' suffixes do not occur.
245:
The root khī is used in the sense of exhaustion. Khīṇoti, khīṇāti—it is exhausted. Birth (jāti) is exhausted. Khīṇo—exhaustion. Due to the lack of effort, there is the exhaustion of wisdom.

The root ge is used in the sense of making a sound. Giṇoti, giṇāti—he speaks.

The root ci is used in the sense of accumulation. In this case, the cerebral ṇ is changed to the dental n. Pākāraṃ cināti—he builds a wall. Kusalaṃ citaṃ—merit is accumulated. Ceto puggalo (A person who builds/accumulates).

The root ru is used in the sense of distress. Ruṇoti, ruṇāti—he is distressed.

The roots rādha and sādha are used in the sense of completion. Rādhuṇāti, sādhuṇāti—it is completed. Rādhanam, ārādhanam, sādhanam—completion/accomplishment.

The root pī is used in the sense of delight. Pīṇoti, pīṇāti—he pleases. Pīti—delight; piyo—dear/beloved.

The roots apa and sambhu are used in the sense of reaching and completion. Pāpuṇoti, pāpuṇāti—he reaches. Patto—reached. The Buddha has reached omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa). He has reached the realm of Yama. Sambhuṇāti—he reaches or attains. He does not reach or complete even a small benefit. Sambhuṇanto, abhisambhuṇamāno—one who reaches.

In the word 'patto', the 'pa' is a prefix (upasagga) as in 'pappoti'. In that case, in the word 'patto', which has the meaning of 'pāpuṇi', when the 'pa' of the root 'ap' (preceded by 'pa') is dropped, the suffix 'ta' is doubled (dvi-bhāva). In that passage, 'na abhisambhuṇāti' means he does not reach or does not complete.

The root khipa is used in the sense of throwing. Khipuṇāti—he throws. Khippaṃ—quickly. 'Khippaṃ' also refers to a fish-trap.

The root āpa is used in the sense of pervading. Āpuṇāti—it pervades. Āpo—water.

The root mi is used in the sense of inserting. Minoti—he inserts. Mitto—a friend.

In this context, one is called 'mitto' (friend) because all secrets are inserted or cast into them. However, the saying 'A friend is indeed made by walking seven steps together' is spoken by way of worldly convention, not by way of literal meaning. If it were spoken by way of literal meaning, then any person...
246:
...who is not intimate or even an opponent would be called a friend, but it should not be regarded so. It should be regarded thus: "Even by walking just seven steps together, by uttering pleasant words to the companion, and by merely engaging in mutual conversation, one is called a friend." Why is that? Would a person who is firmly intimate not be called a friend? (Indeed, they would). This statement is to be understood as being made by way of praising the virtues of a friend.

The root vu is used in the sense of covering (restraining/guarding). It has the forms vuṇoti, vuṇāti, saṃvuṇoti, saṃvuṇāti. The wise man is restrained by virtue (sīlasaṃvuto).

The root su is used in the sense of flowing (pressing, churning, connecting, or bathing). It has the forms suṇoti, suṇāti.

The root si is used in the sense of binding. It has the form sinoti.

The root si is used in the sense of sharpening. It has the forms siṇoti, siṇāti. 'Nisitassatthaṃ' means a sharpened weapon.

This hunchback woman who speaks such evil words,
By a well-sharpened weapon,
Will surely have her tongue cut off.
In this context, 'bhaṇaṃ' means 'bhaṇantī' (one who speaks).
