The root vusa is used in the sense of arrogance. Arrogance means the state of being bold and rude in body, speech, and mind. It has the form vusuṇāti.

The root asu is used in the sense of pervading. It has the form asuṇāti. There is the word 'assu' (tears).

The root hi is used in the senses of going, knowing, and distress. It has the form hinoti.

In this context, a collection of roots that have the same meaning, even if they have different final consonants, is mentioned.

The roots tika, tiga, sagha, dikkha, kivu, ciri, jiri, dāsa, and du are used in the sense of harming. They have the forms tikuṇāti, tiguṇāti, saghuṇāti, dikkhuṇāti.
247:
Kivuṇāti, ciruṇāti, jiruṇāti, dāsuṇāti, duṇoti, and duṇāti—these forms express the meaning of harming (hiṃsā).

I have shown these roots belonging to the Svādi group according to my ability by looking into the Suttas. You also should look for other roots in the Suttas and accept them according to their meaning and logic.

## This is the Svādi Group.

## Roots in the Kiyādi Group

The root kī is used in the sense of exchange of goods (dabbavinimaya). The exchange of goods by means of buying and selling is called 'dabbavinimaya'. Kiṇāti, kiṇanti (he buys, they buy). Vikkiṇāti, vikkiṇanti (he sells, they sell). To buy: ketuṃ, kiṇituṃ. To sell: vikkhetuṃ, vikkiṇituṃ. Having bought: kiṇitvā; having sold: vikkiṇitvā. Goods that are bought: kītaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ. Buying: kayo; selling: vikkayo. (The master) may sell (me) or may kill (me).

The root khi is used in the sense of going (gati). Khiṇāti (it goes). An arrow that has gone far: atikhīṇo saro. Heaven is 'khaṃ'; heavens are 'khāni'. The dental n must be changed to the cerebral ṇ.

In that context, 'khiṇāti' means it goes (gacchati). 'Atikhīṇo' means one that has gone far (atigato). In this regard, there is the Pāli: "They lie like arrows that have gone far from the bow (fallen on the ground and eaten by termites), lamenting over things enjoyed in the past." In that Pāli, 'cāpātikhīṇā' means arrows that have gone far from the bow, or have been released. In the Commentary, however, it is explained as: "'Cāpātikhīṇā' means arrows that have gone far from the bow, or are freed from the bow." That explanation should also be understood as being made by way of intended meaning, referring to the sense of going. In that context, 'khaṃ' means heaven. That heaven is called 'khaṃ' because it is a place to be gone to by those who have performed merit. 'Khāni' means heavens.

The root ci is used in the sense of accumulation (caya). He accumulates merit (puññaṃ cināti). He builds a wall (pākāraṃ cināti). He collects the perfections (pāramiyo vicināti or vicinati). He plucks a flower (pupphaṃ ocināti or ocinati). He arranges or strings together (pacināti). Having arranged (pacinitvā). Merit that is accumulated: citaṃ kusalaṃ. A heap: cayo; an accumulation: sañcayo. A wall that is built: cito pākāro. Because he builds/arranges, he is called 'ceto' (a mason/builder). Any being who...
248:
## Puññasañcaya
"Sañcaya" means accumulation, collection, heap, group, Saṅgha, mass, assembly, cluster, bunch, and so on; these are its synonyms.

The root *ji* is used in the sense of victory. *Jināti* (he conquers), *vijināti* (he conquers specifically), *jiniyati* (it is conquered). *Jetā* (a conqueror), *Jina* (The Conqueror/The Buddha). "Māra is conquered." "He conquered Māra." *Jitavā* (one who has conquered), *jitāvī* (one who has conquered), *jitabba* (to be conquered), *jeyya* (to be conquered/victory), *jayana* (conquering), *jita* (conquered), *vijita* (conquered), *jaya* (victory), *parājayana* (defeat), *parājaya* (defeat). "Whose victory [over defilements] is not turned back into defeat; in this world, no one follows that conquered [defilement] back to him." "This is the victory of the glorious Buddha, and the defeat of the Evil Māra."

Among those terms, "Jetā" refers to anyone who conquers. "Jina" refers to the Omniscient King of Dhamma because he has conquered. What did he conquer? He conquered evil, unwholesome states and enemies such as Māra. Thus, he is called *Jina* because he conquered evil, unwholesome states and enemies like Māra. It is also said:
"Upaka, those like me are indeed Conquerors (Jinas), who have attained the destruction of the taints (āsavas). I have conquered evil states; therefore, I am a Conqueror (Jina)."
And: "Monks, the Tathāgata is the overcomer, the unovercome."

In fact, the word "Jina" used alone refers only to the Omniscient Buddha. When used with a prefix, it applies to Paccekabuddhas and others, as well as to the Omniscient Buddha, as appropriate. Examples include: "Paccekajina, Odhisajina, Anodhisajina, Vipākajina, Avipākajina."

The root *ji* is also used in the sense of loss or depletion. *Jināti* (he loses), *na jināti na jāpaye* (he does not lose, nor causes to lose). He loses (gives up) chariot horses and jeweled earrings; likewise, he loses sons and wives. He loses wealth and slaves.
249:
The root *ñā* is used in the sense of knowing. *Jānāti* (he knows), *ñāyati* (it is known), *nāyati* (it is known). It is used as: "Being without signs, they are not known," and "If he should neglect his energy, he should be known [as a lazy person]," and "He desires: 'Let them not know me [as an evildoer].'" Because of the sense of being known as "these are our own people," they are called *ñāti* (relative) or *ñātaka* (kinsman). It is also used in: "Relatives, friends, and those of good heart," and "Our kinsman is sitting," etc. That which is to be known is called *ñeyya* (the knowable); these are formations (saṅkhāra), variations (vikāra), characteristics (lakkhaṇa), Nibbāna, and concepts (paññatti). In such contexts, the word *ñeyya* is strictly neuter, but when used as an adjective (vaccum-liṅga), it takes all three genders. For example: *ñeyyo phasso* (knowable contact), *ñeyyā vedanā* (knowable feeling), *ñeyyaṃ cittaṃ* (knowable mind), *ñeyyo puriso* (knowable man), *ñeyyā itthī* (knowable woman), *ñeyyaṃ dhanaṃ* (knowable wealth).

The root *thu* is used in the sense of praise. *Thunāti*, *abhitthunāti* (he praises). *Thuti*, *abhitthuti*, *thavanā*, *abhitthavanā* (praise/extolling), *thuto*, *abhitthuto* (praised).

The root *thu* is also used in the sense of lamentation. *Thunāti* (he laments/groans). It is used as: "Arise, Revatī of very evil nature, you who have no closed door [to hell] for those who receive gifts (or whose door to hell is open), and who are without charity and virtue. We shall lead you to the hell where the miserable ones, filled with suffering, groan," and "Lamenting over things enjoyed in the past."

The root *du* is used in the sense of harming. *Dunāti* (he harms). Examples are *mittaddu* (one who betrays a friend) and *duma* (tree). Here, *mittaddu* is so called because he harms, wrongs, or betrays a friend. The Pali reference here is: "The Vedas are not for the protection of that man who betrays a friend and destroys growth (bhūnahu)." *Duma* (tree) is so called because it is harmed or cut down for the sake of house materials, etc., or it is oppressed by those desiring leaves and flowers by the taking of those leaves and flowers.

The root *dhū* is used in the sense of shaking. *Dhunāti* (he shakes). *Dhūmo* (smoke), *dhonā* (wisdom), *dhono* (a wise person), *dhuto* (shaken off). It is used as: "Shaking the bark-fiber garments, I then go through the sky."
250:
In those passages, "dhūma" is so called because it shakes or is shaken. The word *dhūma* is used in the senses of anger, craving, thought (vitakka), the five cords of sensual pleasure, Dhamma teaching, and natural smoke. In the passage "Anger is smoke, false speech is ashes," it is used in the sense of anger. In "Always burning with the smoke of desire," it is used in the sense of craving. In "At that time, a certain monk was sitting not far from the Blessed One, 'smoking' [with unwholesome thoughts]," it is used in the sense of thought.

"O King Brahmadatta, sensual pleasures are a swamp, a great swamp. I have called this sensual state a great danger with three roots. I have also declared it to be like dust and like smoke. Therefore, give up those sensual pleasures and go forth [as a monk]."
In this passage, it is used in the sense of the five cords of sensual pleasure. In "He becomes a maker of smoke," it is used in the sense of Dhamma teaching. In "The banner is the sign of the chariot, smoke is the sign of fire," it is used in the sense of natural smoke.

Thus:
The word *dhūma* occurs in the senses of anger, craving, and thought,
In the five cords of sensual pleasure,
In teaching, and in natural smoke.

"Dhonā" means wisdom. This was said in the Niddesa: "Wisdom is called *dhonā*; that wisdom which is discerning, which is Right View. Why is wisdom called *dhonā*? Because by that wisdom, bodily misconduct is shaken off (*dhuta*), washed (*dhota*), cleansed (*sandhota*), and purged (*niddhāta*); verbal misconduct and mental misconduct are shaken off, washed, cleansed, and purged. For that reason, wisdom is called *dhonā*. Alternatively, Right View has shaken off, washed, cleansed, and purged Wrong View; for that reason, wisdom is called *dhonā*." The Pali reference here is: "For the wise one (*dhona*), there is nowhere in the world any concocted view regarding various states of existence."
251:
This Pali text serves as an illustration (nidassana) here. In this context, because of the sense 'wisdom (dhonā) exists in him,' he is called 'Dhona'; this is the etymological derivation (nibbacana) of the word Dhona. Due to the multiple meanings of roots, the root dhū occurs in the sense of trembling as well as in the sense of washing or cleansing.

The root mun occurs in the sense of knowing (ñāṇa). There are forms such as munāti (he knows), monaṃ (knowing), and muni (one who knows). In this context, when the root is in the form of a finite verb, the elision of the final consonant (na) invariably occurs. However, in the verse of Elder Sobhita, in the future tense, due to the strengthening (vuddhi) of the vowel 'u', another form is seen: 'I shall know by means of knowledge (monena monissaṃ).' There, 'monissaṃ' means 'I shall know (jānissaṃ).' In the noun form, the elision of the final consonant does not occur. In that context, although 'mona' is said to be 'silence (tuṇhībhāva)' in the passage 'Not by silence does one become a sage,' here, because it is stated as 'ñāṇa' (knowledge), that silence is not intended; only knowledge is intended. Therefore, 'mona' which is the path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa) described as the practice of a sage (moneyya-paṭipadā) should also be taken.

'Muni' means one who knows what is beneficial and what is not, and who discriminates; thus, he is called a Muni. Alternatively, just as one weighs things on a scale in the world, he knows these two meanings by way of 'these are internal aggregates, these are external aggregates,' and so on; thus, he is called a Muni. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

'Not by silence does a foolish, ignorant person become a sage.
But the wise man who, as if holding a pair of scales, takes what is noble,
And avoids evils—he is a sage; for that reason, he is a sage.
He who knows both worlds is called a sage for that reason.'

There is also another explanation of the meaning for this term Muni. 'Muni' means knowledge is called 'mona,' or it refers to one of the practices such as bodily sage-hood (kāya-moneyya); because he is endowed with that knowledge or bodily sage-hood, etc., the person is called a 'Muni.' That Muni is of various types: the lay sage (agāriya-muni), the homeless sage (anagāriya-muni), the trainee sage (sekkha-muni), the adept sage (asekkha-muni), the solitary sage (pacceka-muni), and the Sage of sages (munimuni, i.e., the Buddha).
252:
The Muni is of many kinds. Among those Munis, the 'lay sage' (agāriya-muni) is a layperson who has attained the paths and fruits and has understood the Dispensation. The 'homeless sage' (anagāriya-muni) is a monk of such a nature. The 'trainee sage' (sekkha-muni) refers to the seven types of trainees (sekkhas). The 'adept sage' (asekkha-muni) is the Arahant. The 'solitary sage' (pacceka-muni) refers to the Paccekabuddhas. The 'Sage of sages' (munimuni) refers to the Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas (Sammāsambuddhas). For this very reason, the Venerable Sāriputta also said: 'The Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is called a Muni.'

The root pū occurs in the sense of purifying (pavana). Purifying is pavana or sodhana. Punāti means he purifies. There are terms such as puñña (merit), putta (son), and dantapoṇa (tooth-wood).

Among these terms, 'puñña' is so called because it cleanses or purifies the one who performs it. Alternatively, it is called puñña because it cleanses or purifies the mental continuum in which it has arisen. What is that puñña? It is wholesome kamma (kusala-kamma) well-practiced. Since the root pū is a transitive verb, the explanation of its meaning can be obtained through the causative sense.

'Putta' is so called because he cleanses or purifies his own lineage. If 'putta' were defined only as one who cleanses his lineage, it should not be said that those of low birth, such as outcasts (caṇḍālas), cannot have a son; this is because the expression of the meaning of words occurs in various ways. Therefore, the derivation should also be taken as 'putta' because he fills the heart of his father, and so on. Indeed, words achieve their completion through various roots.

A son (putta) is of four kinds: the biological son (atraja), the son of the field (khettaja), the resident pupil (antevāsika), and the adopted son (dinnaka). Among these four, the son born depending on oneself is called 'atraja.' The son born on a bed, a stool, a couch, or in the lap, etc., is called 'khettaja.' One who learns an art or craft in one's presence is called 'antevāsika.' One who is given for the purpose of being raised is called 'dinnaka.' 'Dantapoṇa' is so called because one cleanses or purifies the teeth with this object; it refers to the tooth-wood (dantakaṭṭha).

The root pī occurs in the senses of satisfaction and delight. Piṇāti means he delights; hence it is called 'pīti' (rapture). In this term, 'pīti' means delighting, and it is also said to mean satisfaction and fondness. This is the derivation by way of the state of being (bhāva).
253:
However, by way of the causative agent (hetu-kattu), it is called 'pīti' because it causes (beings) to delight (piṇayati); it means it causes satisfaction. That rapture (pīti) is of five kinds: minor rapture (khuddaka-pīti), momentary rapture (khaṇika-pīti), showering rapture (okkantika-pīti), uplifting rapture (ubbegā-pīti), and pervading rapture (pharaṇā-pīti). Among these five, minor rapture is only able to cause the raising of the body hairs. Momentary rapture is like a flash of lightning in each moment. Showering rapture breaks over the body again and again like waves on the seashore. Uplifting rapture is powerful and has the magnitude to lift the body up and cause it to leap into the air. When pervading rapture arises, it stays pervading and filling the entire body, like a bladder filled with blown air, or like a mountain cavern into which a great flood of water has rushed. Thus, rapture is of five kinds. Because that rapture has the characteristic of being very pleasing, it is also proper to call it 'pīti' by way of the simple agent (suddha-kattu) as 'piṇāti' (it delights). In this context, words such as 'piyāyati' (he cherishes), 'pitā' (father), 'piyo' (dear one), and 'pemo' (love/affection) are forms of the root pī itself. Among those words, they say: 'He is called a father (pitā) because he cherishes his son.' Because he is to be cherished, he is called 'piyo.' Loving is 'pemo.'

The root mā occurs in the sense of measuring (parimāṇa). Mināti means he measures. There are terms such as māna, parimāṇa, matta, mattā, mano, vimāna, minitabba, metabba, and 'chāyā metabbā' (the shadow should be measured). In such instances, the suffix 'aniya' is not obtained.

In this context, 'mano' (mind) is so called because it measures or delimits the object, just as one measures with a measuring cup (nāḷi) or a pair of scales. 'Vimāna' (mansion) is so called because it is specially measured or delimited; it is a celestial abode or divine palace arisen by the power of the merit of the devas. It is also called vimāna because it is praised as 'this celestial mansion is beautiful and radiant,' and so on. The root mī occurs in the sense of harming (hiṃsā). Mināti means he harms. There are terms such as mīna (fish) and kumīna (fish-trap).
254:
In this context, 'mīna' means fish. Indeed, fish have many names such as mīna, maccha, ambuja, vārija, and vāricara. Specific names include amara (eel or sturgeon), khalisa (snakehead fish), candakula (sandalwood fish), kandaphali, indaphali, indavala, kulisa, vāmi, kuṅkutala, kaṇḍika (thorny fish), sakula, maṅgura (catfish), siṅgī (horned fish or shark), satavaṅka (eel), rohita (carp), pāṭhīna (sheatfish), kāṇa (blind fish), savaṅka (snake-fish), pāvusa, and so forth. There are also names like timi and timiṅgala. 'Kumīna' refers to a device used to harm fish in a loathsome manner; therefore, it is called kumīna (a fish trap or cage). This trap is referred to by the word 'kumīna' in the Pali texts. Accordingly, the following Pali passage is found: 'Just as a fisherman strikes a fish bound in the mouth of a trap, so this Brahmin reviles and strikes my beloved sons and daughters while I, though present, do not see them.'

The root 'mu' is used in the sense of binding. 'Munāti' means he binds. Therefore, he is called 'muni'. In this context, 'muni' is so called because he binds his own mind, not allowing it to go under the influence of passion, hatred, and so forth.

The root 'ri' is used in the senses of going and preaching. 'Rikāti' means he goes or he preaches. 'Reṇu' (dust or pollen). The letter 'n' is changed to 'ṇ'.

The root 'lī' is used in the sense of clinging. 'Lināti' means he clings; 'nilināti' means he rests or dwells. 'Līna' (hiding), 'sallīna' (indwelling or seclusion), 'paṭisallāna' (solitude or retirement).

The root 'vī' is used in the sense of weaving threads. 'Vatthaṃ vināti' means he weaves cloth. 'Weave a robe with this thread.' In the passive voice: 'Friends, this robe is woven intended for me.' 'Vīta' (woven). 'Suvīta' (well-woven). 'The weaving to be done is little.' In the causative: 'vāyāpeti' (he causes to weave), as in 'We shall cause the robe to be woven by weavers' or 'They caused the robe to be woven,' and so forth.

The root 'vī' is used in the sense of harming. 'Vināti' means he harms. 'Veṇu' (bamboo). 'Veṇu' refers to the bamboo plant.
255:
The root 'lu' is used in the sense of cutting. 'Lunāti' means he cuts. From this, words such as 'loṇa' (salt), 'kusala' (wholesome/merit), 'bāla' (fool), and 'lūta' (spider) are derived.

Among these terms, 'loṇa' is so called because it destroys the tasteless state and creates its own salty state; thus it is 'loṇa' or 'lavaṇa' (salt). 'Kusala' is so called because it cuts off unwholesome states just as kusa grass cuts the palm of the hand. It refers to states characterized by faultlessness and the production of pleasant results. 'Bāla' (fool) is so called because he cuts off benefits in both the present life and the future life. 'Lūta' refers to a spider. The thread of that spider is called 'lūtasutta'. It is called 'lūta' because it lives by cutting the life of insects such as grasshoppers and flies to drink their essence.

The root 'si' is used in the sense of binding. 'Sināti' means he binds. From this, 'sīmā' (boundary) and 'sīsa' (head) are derived.

In this context, 'sīmā' is so called because it is bound by the unified Saṅgha through a formal act (kammavācā). That sīmā is of two types: baddha-sīmā (bound boundary) and abaddha-sīmā (unbound boundary). Among these, abaddha-sīmā should be understood as a 'boundary' by virtue of making a demarcation. 'Sīsa' (head) is so called because it is the part where hair is bound by virtue of making a topknot. Other forms should also be applied in this manner.

The root 'sā' is used in the sense of cooking. 'Sināti' means he cooks.

The root 'su' is used in the sense of harming. 'Suṇāti' means he harms. 'Parasu' (axe). It is called 'parasu' because one harms others (or harms greatly) with this object.

The root 'as' is used in the sense of eating. He eats the fruits of the plants that have been sown. 'Asana' (food/meal).

In this context, 'asana' refers to nutriment. It is called 'asana' because it is eaten (asiyati). The phrase 'Eat, chew, drink' serves as an example here.

The root 'kilisa' is used in the sense of afflicting or oppressing. 'Kilisnāti' means he afflicts or oppresses. 'Kilesa' (defilement).

In this context, 'kilesa' refers to passion (rāga) and the like, as well as to suffering (dukkha).

The root 'uddhasa' is used in the sense of seeking. 'Uñcha' means seeking or gleaning. 'Uddhasnāti' means he seeks.
256:
The root 'isa' is used in the sense of occurring constantly. 'Isnāti' means it occurs constantly.

The root 'visa' is used in the sense of separation. 'Visnāti' means he is separated. 'Visa' (poison).

The root 'pusa' is used in the senses of flowing and filling. 'Pusnāti' means it fills.

The root 'pusa' is used in the sense of nourishing. 'Pusnāti' means he nourishes.

The root 'musa' is used in the sense of stealing. 'Musnāti' means he steals. 'Musala' (pestle).

I have seen this many roots belonging to the Kiyādi group according to my ability. Having looked for other roots in the Suttas, you should accept them according to the logic of their meaning. These roots are shown from the scriptural texts (Sāsana) and worldly texts. Among them, those from worldly texts are mentioned because they are consistent with the Sāsana and serve to benefit the Sāsana.

## This is the Kiyādi Group.

## The Gahādi Group

Now the Gahādi group will be discussed. In this group, some teachers think as follows: A group called 'Gahādi' (roots starting with 'gah') is not found separately (from the Kiyādi group). How can the single root 'gah' constitute the Gahādi group? From which root in the Buddha's Dispensation (Jinasāsana) should the suffixes 'ppa' and 'ṇhā' follow? There are no others besides the root 'gah'. Thinking thus, some teachers include the root 'gah' within the Kiyādi group. In this way, they do not speak of a separate Gahādi group. A wise person who reflects well should not accept the view of those teachers. This is because the Gahādi group is mentioned separately in the Kaccāyana grammar. Indeed, the teacher Kaccāyana, who stated the rule 'Gahādito ppaṇhā', has shown the Gahādi group separately in the Sāsana, has he not?
257: If a separate group (gaᅉa) of roots such as gah is not obtained; and if one discards this external word ‘ādi’ in the rule indicating the gahādi group; then it should only be said ‘gahato ppaᅉhā’, or else a single rule ‘kiyādito nāppaᅉhā’ should be made. Since it is not said ‘gahato ppaᅉhā’, nor is a single rule made, therefore this gahādi group should be known as a group distinct from kiyādi. Like the rules ‘sarā sare lopaᅃ’ etc., this rule is profound; it is difficult to understand for one who merely speculates without traditional logic. In that rule ‘gahādito ppaᅉhā’, the inclusion of the word ‘ādi’ is made with reference to roots like us etc. For that reason, forms like ‘uᅉhāpeti’ etc. are seen. Now, making clear the benefit of the word ‘ādi’, I shall speak of the group of roots starting with gah along with their applications; listen to my words. The root gah is in the sense of grasping (upādāna). Grasping means taking, not the grasping of defilements (kilesupādāna). Here, the prefix ‘upa’ does not express any special meaning. Alternatively, taking by approaching with body or mind is called upādāna; thus the prefix ‘upa’ has the sense of ‘near’. In some terms like ‘kāmupādāna’, the prefix ‘upa’ together with the word ‘ādāna’ exists in the sense of firm grasping. But here, whether it be firm grasping or loose grasping, any kind of taking is indeed upādāna; therefore, the meaning should be taken that the root gah exists in the sense of taking. Gheppati, gaᅉhāti (takes). Pariggaᅉhāti, paᅡiggaᅉhāti, adhigaᅉhāti, paggaᅉhāti, niggaᅉhāti. One who takes predominantly. To take, to learn. Having taken, having learned. There are also other forms. I will take the net. To take. Having taken. One who learns, one who collects, one who has entered. In the causative: ‘gaᅉhāpeti, gaᅉhāpayati’, ‘they cause to learn another foundation of mindfulness’, ‘having caused to take along with a thousand ministers’. ‘The preceptor should be caused to take’. Preceptor...
258: (In the sense of causing to take) Having caused to take. He causes to take, he causes to take, he will cause to take. They cause to take their own nature. One who takes, having caused to take, etc. In the passive sense: it is taken, it is collected, or it is taken. For that reason, in the Niddesa Pali, it is seen: ‘they are taken, they are learned’. Terms such as ‘house (geha), taking (gāha), possession (pariggaha), one who collects (saᅃgāhaka), one who treats kindly (saᅃgahetā)’ should be applied. In that (root gah), for words ending in the suffix -ti immediately following the letter ‘a’, the paradigm (padamālā) should be applied in all inflections and in all ways, such as ‘gheppati, gheppanti, gheppasi’ and ‘gaᅉhati, gaᅉhanti, gaᅉhasi’. For words ending in the suffix -ti immediately following the letters ‘ā’ or ‘e’, the paradigm should be applied as appropriate, such as ‘gaᅉhāti, gaᅉhāpeti’, excluding the places that should be excluded. These are some well-known aorist (ajjatanĩ) forms: ‘he took the clay bowl’, ‘they took’, ‘they took’, ‘they took’. In the future (bhavissantĩ) etc., there are ‘gahessati, gahessanti’. The rest should be completed. There are ‘aggahissā, aggahissaᅃsu’. The rest should be completed. The root us is in the sense of burning. Burning is called uᅉha (heat). It burns, therefore it is called uᅉha. The word uᅉha refers to a substance in phrases like ‘he eats hot rice’, but in phrases like ‘he dispels cold with heat’, it refers to a quality because the state of being hot is intended. Indeed, the state of being hot and the state of being cold are qualities. The root tas is in the sense of thirst. Taᅉhā (craving). In what sense is it called taᅉhā? In the sense that it thirsts, it thirsts repeatedly. The root jusi is in the senses of delight and service. The bright fortnight (juᅉha-samaya). Whether in the dark or in the bright (fortnight), when the wind blows. There, juᅉha means it causes delight and joy to the world; therefore it is called juᅉha.
259: The root jut is in the sense of shining. Juᅉhā-ratti means a night associated with moonlight. Although it has no light of its own, it is called juᅉhā because it shines, glows, and becomes luminous with the light of the moon and stars. The root sā is in the sense of making thin (refining). Saᅉha-vācā means gentle speech. It is called saᅉhā because it is made thin and refined, not made harsh by a coarse nature. The root so is in the sense of making an end. Saᅉhaᅃ 1āᅉaᅃ means subtle wisdom. It is called saᅉhaᅃ because, by its own subtle nature, it brings even very subtle meanings to an end or brings them to completion. The root tij is in the sense of sharpness. Nisāna means the state of being sharp. Tiᅉho parasu means a sharp axe. It is called tiᅉho because it is sharp. The root si is in the sense of service. It is called sippa (art/craft) because it is resorted to by those desiring their own welfare. Any field of knowledge to be learned for the sake of livelihood is called sippāyatana. Furthermore, sippa refers to the eighteen great arts: the Vedas, Law (Dhammasatta), Grammar, Prosody, Etymology, Astronomy, Phonetics, Means of release, Ritual (Kriyāvidhi), Archery, Elephant lore, Erotics, Horsemanship, Puranas, History, Ethics (Nĩti), Logic, and Medicine. The root ku is in the sense of contempt. Kucchā means contempt. Kaᅉhā dhammā means dark states (unwholesome states). Kaᅉho puriso means a dark man. There, kaᅉhā refers to unwholesome states that should be despised and blamed by the wise because they cause a lack of radiance. Kaᅉho refers to a dark complexion which, when compared to a golden complexion etc., is to be despised and blamed. It is also said: ‘This man is indeed dark; he eats dark food; in a dark place (he lives); he is not dear to my mind.’
260:
“One is not dark by skin; a Brahmin is one who has inner essence (virtue, etc.). He in whom evil deeds exist, he indeed is dark, O Sujampati,” said the King of Devas.

Thus—
In the group of roots beginning with 'gaha', the word 'ādi' (etc.) is used with reference to the root 'tas' and others. In the roots beginning with 'gaha', the suffixes '-ppa' and '-ṇhā' are applied as appropriate. The suffix '-ppa' following the root 'gaha' is evident only in the verbal form (ākhyāta). The suffix '-ṇhā' following the root 'us' is evident in both verbal and nominal forms. Following roots other than 'us' and 'gaha', these two suffixes should be understood as occurring only in nominal forms. Thus, the determination of the Gahādi group should be specifically understood.

In this regard, although the verbal form 'taṇhāyati' is found in the Dispensation (Sāsana), it cannot be said that it primarily takes the '-ṇhā' suffix, because like 'pabbatāyati' and 'mettāyati', it is accomplished by the power of the '-āya' suffix prescribed after a noun-stem. In fact, this word 'taṇhāyati' is formed by the power of the '-āya' suffix following the word 'taṇhā', which itself is derived from the root 'tas' with the '-ṇhā' suffix. Similarly, although the causative verbal form 'uṇhāpeti' is found in the commentary on the Rūpiyasaṃvohāra training rule of the Vinaya in the passage, “Having heated the blade of an adze, he heats either water or milk,” it cannot be said that it primarily takes the '-ṇhā' suffix, even though it is a verbal form, because it is accomplished by the power of the causative suffix named '-ṇāpe' prescribed after the word 'uṇha', which is derived from the root 'us' with the '-ṇhā' suffix. This word 'uṇhāpeti' is formed from the aforementioned word 'uṇha' by the power of the '-ṇāpe' suffix; when this word is seen, the word 'uṇhāpayati' is also considered seen.
261:
Furthermore, because the causative form 'uṇhāpeti' is found in the Vinaya Commentary, the simple active form 'uṇhati' is also considered found by way of inference. This is because both simple active and causative forms can be obtained from a single root, for example: 'gaṇhāti, gaṇhāpeti; gacchati, gacchāpeti'. Therefore, knowing that the form 'uṇhati' of the root 'us' (in the sense of burning) can be obtained, the definition should be made as: “It burns, therefore it is called 'uṇha' (hot).” Thus, it should be understood that the suffix '-ppa' is obtained in only one way as a noun from the root 'gaha' and others. The suffix '-ṇhā', however, is obtained in two ways—as both verb and noun—from the roots 'gaha' and 'us', and in only one way as a noun from other roots. Although such a rule is stated here, one should search for two nominal forms and two types of verbal forms (simple and causative) for each of the other roots in the Word of the Buddha (Buddhavacana) together with the Commentaries. We have included the root 'tas' and others in the Gahādi group by the word 'ādi' according to the method consistent with the Word of the Buddha. There is no other method more excellent than this; this method alone is most praiseworthy. Therefore, this system should be well-maintained and taught by the Venerable ones for the stability of the Dispensation.

I have found these Gahādi roots in the Suttas according to my ability. You also should look for other Gahādi roots in the Suttas and accept them according to the logic of the meaning.

## This is the Gahādi Group.

## Tanādi Group

The root 'tanu' is used in the sense of expansion (stretching). 'Tanoti' (he expands/stretches). 'Āyatana', 'tanu' (body). In the passive voice, there are forms such as 'taniyyati' (it is expanded), 'taniyyanti', and 'vitaniyyati'. In this regard, the Pali text is: “Just as an ox-hide is stretched out on the ground (with a hundred pegs).” Teachers, however, mention the forms 'patāyate' and 'pataññati'. 'Tanituṃ', 'tanitvāna', etc., are forms accomplished with the '-tumun' suffix and others.
262:
In that word 'āyatana', it is called 'āyatana' because it expands or extends the states that have arisen (āya). 'Tanu' refers to the body. That body is called 'tanu' because, starting from the embryonic stage (kalala), it is expanded, extended, and brought to greatness by kamma and other factors as applicable. Words such as 'tanu, vapu, sarīra, puṃ, kāya, deha' are terms denoting the body. The body is the collection of the five aggregates. That which the masses call 'the body' is, in the ultimate sense, merely the collection of the five aggregates; other than that, no 'self' (atta) or 'belonging to self' (attaniya) can be found. However, in passages such as “The path-consciousness of the Once-returner (Sakadāgāmi) which makes thin (tanu) sensual lust and ill-will,” the word 'tanu' denotes the meaning of 'scant' or 'thin' (appattha). Since no verbal form is found for this 'tanu' which denotes the meaning of 'thin', it should be an indeclinable (nipāta). Although we do not find a place where it is explicitly stated that the word 'tanu' is an indeclinable, it should be accepted by determination as an underived stem (anipphanna-pāṭipadika) not formed by grammatical analysis of roots and suffixes.

Tanoti, tanonti. Tanosi, tanotha. Tanomi, tanoma. Tanute, tanunte. Tanuse, tanuse, tanuvhe. Tane, tanumhe. The remaining forms should be expanded as applicable.

Tanotu, tanontu. Taneyya, tane, taneyyuṃ. Vitana, vitanu. Atanā, atanu. 'Ammāya patanu kesā' (The mother's hairs are thin). Atani, ataniṃsu. Tanissati, tanissanti. Atanissā, atanissaṃsu. In the passive form, it should be expanded as 'taniyyati, taniyyanti, taniyyasi', and so on.

The root 'sak' is used in the sense of ability (satti). 'Satti' means the state of being capable (samattha-bhāva). Because of the meaning 'he is able', he is called 'Sakka' (the King of Devas). 'Asakkhi' (he was able to make known). 'Sakkhissasi' (you will be able). 'Sakkhati' (he is able). “Mother, you too will be able to ordain.” “It is possible to counteract old age,” so says the Pali.
263:
Among those terms, 'Sakka' refers to the King of Devas. He is called 'Sakka' because he is capable of performing his own and others' welfare, being able to contemplate even a thousand of his own interests in a single moment. Alternatively, by the power of a derivative (taddhita) which is not the scope of roots, he gave gifts respectfully (sakkaccaṃ); thus, taking this meaning, the word 'Sakka' should be established according to the method of etymology (nirutti). Indeed, the Blessed One said, 'Mahāli, Sakka, the King of Devas, when he was a human being in the past, gave gifts respectfully; therefore, he is called Sakka.' A capable man, a capable woman, a capable family.

The roots 'khuṇu' and 'khiṇu' are used in the sense of harming. Khuṇoti, khiṇoti.

The root 'iṇu' is used in the sense of going. Iṇoti. Debt (iṇa), creditor (iṇāyika).

The root 'tiṇu' is used in the sense of eating. Tiṇoti. Grass (tiṇa). Here, 'tiṇa' means grass. It is called 'tiṇa' because it is eaten (khādiyati) by grass-eating animals such as oxen.

The root 'ghiṇu' is used in the sense of splendor. Ghiṇoti.

The root 'hanu' is used in the sense of removing or silence. Silence means not speaking or making oneself wordless. Hanoti, hanute.

The root 'panu' is used in the sense of giving. Panoti, panute.

The root 'manu' is used in the sense of knowing. Manoti, manute. Mind (mano), mind (manaṃ), mental state (mānasaṃ), human (manusso), youth (mānavo), youth (māṇavo).

Here, 'mano' is so called because it knows (manute); 'manaṃ' is the same. Regarding these two words for mind, their masculine and neuter genders should be understood in passages such as 'In whom the mind (mano) enters; his mind (manaṃ) becomes peaceful.' The word 'mānasa' signifies lust (rāga), the mind (citta), and also Arahatship (arahatta). In the passage, 'The snare of lust (mānasa) that moves in the sky, moves (exists),' lust is called 'mānasa'. In 'Citta, mano, mānasa,' the mind is called 'mānasa'. In 'The learner (sekha) who has not yet reached Arahatship (appattamānaso), though famous among people, might die,' Arahatship is called 'mānasa'.
264:
In this (Mahāvagga Pali), 'mānasa' refers to lust in the phrase 'yvāyaṃ carati mānaso'. In this (Dhammasaṅgaṇī Pali), 'mānasa' refers to the mind in the phrase 'cittaṃ mano mānasaṃ'. In this (Mārasaṃyutta Pali), 'mānasa' refers to the fruit of Arahatship in the phrase 'appattamānaso sekkho, kālaṃ kayirā jane suto'. Regarding this, it is said:

Lust, the mind, and Arahatship are called 'mānasa' in the teaching of the Teacher, which disciplines evil (or is not wicked) and disciplines the entire thicket of defilements.

Among those three, lust is called 'mānaso' because it arises in the associated mind. The mind itself is called 'mānasaṃ' by defining it as 'mano eva mānasaṃ'. The path of Arahatship (aggamagga) is called 'mānasaṃ' because it completely cuts off (samucchindati) conceit (māna). The fruit of Arahatship should be understood as 'mānasa' because it is produced by that path of Arahatship.

'Manu' means a living being. In the Pali, 'By which eye-sensitivity a being (manu) sees forms,' 'manu' means a living being. Alternatively, 'Manu' is the name of the man who stood in the position of a parent to humans at the beginning of the world-cycle, who is called 'King Mahāsammata' in the Dispensation. He is called 'Manu' because he knows (manute) how to perform the welfare of the entire world.

One is called 'manussa' (human) because one knows one's own welfare according to one's strength. Or, one is called 'manussa' because of the superiority of the mind (knowledge or wholesome mind). Alternatively, one is called 'manussa' because of being the offspring of the aforementioned King Manu. Similarly, 'mānava' and 'māṇava' are formed; when the letter 'n' is changed to 'ṇ', the form 'māṇava' is accomplished.

Some teachers say, 'The word mānava with the dental n is a common term for all beings, while the word māṇava with the retroflex ṇ refers to a contemptible person, a confused youth, or a being.' This should be considered and accepted if appropriate. However, it should not be said that 'this statement is contradictory in extracting the meaning of the word māṇava.' This is because, in extracting the meaning of the word 'antara', the words 'antara' and 'antarikā' are also seen to be brought forth.
265:
In this matter, there is this investigation: In the Cūḷakammavibhaṅga Sutta, regarding the phrase 'the young man Subha, son of Todeyya,' the commentators (Aṭṭhakathācariyas) stated, 'Subha was said to be beautiful and inspiring; therefore, because of the beauty of his limbs, they named him Subha. He was called māṇava in his youth, and even in his old age, he was referred to by that same term.' Thus, the meaning of the word 'māṇava' with the retroflex ṇ is explained. In the sub-commentary (ṭīkā) of that Sutta, the teachers also stated, 'Whether an offspring is a contemptible thief or a confused youth, the term māṇava is used in the world. Generally, beings are of a confused nature in their youth; thus it was said in the commentary that they called him so in his youth.' Thus, the meaning of the word 'māṇava' with the retroflex ṇ is explained.

Now, the extraction of the meanings of the word 'māṇava' follows. 'Māṇava' refers to a being, a thief, or a youth. In passages such as 'Those māṇavas who, being urged by the divine messengers, are negligent,' 'māṇava' refers to a being. In passages such as 'They go with māṇavas who have committed theft and those who have not,' it refers to a thief. In passages such as 'the young man Ambaṭṭha,' 'māṇava' refers to a youth.

The root 'appa' is used in the sense of reaching. Appoti—reaches. Āpo—water. Here, 'āpo' is so called because it flows to various places.

The root 'mā' is used in the sense of measuring. Minoti—measures. Upamā (simile), upamāna (comparison), vimāna (mansion). Other terms should also be applied in this way.

In this context, that which is close to the object being compared, without being absolutely measured or delimited, is called 'upamā' (simile). An example is 'like a forest ox which is similar to an ox.'
266:
Upamāna means comparison itself. Thus it is said: "(I pay homage to the Buddha) who is beyond comparison, immeasurable, and the protector of those who are helpless." Here, the meaning of the word 'vītopamāna' is one who has no comparison, one who is peerless. Alternatively, upamāna is the mode of comparison as in the phrase "The Blessed One is like a lion." In this example, the lion is the upamāna (the object of comparison), and the Blessed One is the upameyya (the subject of comparison) because He is to be compared by means of His majesty, effort, and so on; majesty, effort, and so on are the modes of comparison. In this context, because of His excellence, even if there is no actual mode of comparison between the majesty of a lion and the majesty of the Blessed One, it should be understood that it is stated as "The Blessed One is like a lion" by way of an inferior comparison. Vimāna (a mansion/celestial palace), although it is produced by climate (utu), is called vimāna because it is specifically measured and delimited by kamma, as it is produced by climate conditioned by kamma.

The root 'kar' is used in the sense of 'doing' (karaṇe). The forms such as karoti, kayirati, kubbati, krubbati, pakaroti, upakaroti, apakaroti, paṭikaroti, nirākaroti, paṭisaṅkharoti, abhisaṅkharoti occur in the active voice (kattari). In the passive voice (kamme), according to the method of the Pali texts, where the augment 'i' occurs, the 'ya' is doubled. In that same place where the augment 'i' occurs, if there is a metathesis (vipariyāya) of 'ra' and 'ya', doubling does not occur. Likewise, where the augment 'ī' occurs, forms such as kariyati, kayirati, karīyati, kayyati, pakarīyati, pakariyati, paṭisaṅkhariyati, abhisaṅkhariyati occur in the passive voice.

In this context, the word 'kayirati' is seen in both places: in the active and in the passive. Among these two, by way of the active voice, it should be applied as "The man does the work"; by way of the passive voice, it is according to this Pali: "A hut was made for me with unprescribed materials." Among those two, the active form mentioned by way of the agent is accomplished with the 'yira' suffix. The passive form mentioned by way of the object should be understood as being accomplished by the metathesis of 'ra' and 'ya', which are the beginning and end of the 'i' augment. The four causative forms (kārita), namely kāreti, kārayati, kārāpeti, and kārāpayati, are called 'hetukattu' forms because they indicate that meaning.
267:
Now, however, the paradigm (padamālā) is to be stated. Therein, first, I shall present the paradigm of the word 'kubbati' alone, as it can be applied in a uniform manner across all cases (using the base 'kubba-'). The paradigms of the word 'karoti', which ends in 'ti' immediately following the vowel 'o', and the word 'kāreti', which ends in 'ti' immediately following the vowel 'e', will be presented later as appropriate, since they cannot be applied in a uniform manner.

In that (paradigm of kubbati): kubbati, kubbanti; kubbasi, kubbatha; kubbāmi, kubbāma; kubbate, kubbante; kubbase, kubbavhe; kubbe, kubbamhe. These are the forms stated by way of the present tense (vattamanā).

By way of the imperative (pañcamī) and so on: kubbatu, kubbantu; kubbeyya, kubbeyyuṃ. The remaining forms should be understood by expanding them in all places according to the method stated for the forms 'bhavati, bhavanti'.

Words ending in 'ti' immediately following the letter 'a', such as 'kariyati', should also be applied in this same way. Here, this paradigm stated as 'kubbati, kubbanti, kubbasi', etc., is stated because such is seen in the method of the Pali texts. However, those members of the Dispensation who are experts in grammar (such as the author of the Rūpasiddhi), giving weight only to the treatises on grammar, do not accept such forms, believing that forms like 'kubbati, kubbasi' do not exist in the Pali texts. They, as in the grammar treatises, believe that in the Pali texts also, in places such as 'asanto nānukubbanti', the letter 'u' which is a substitute for the 'o' suffix becomes the letter 'va' only when a vowel follows; thus they accept only forms like 'kubbanti, kubbante', and do not accept forms like 'kubbati, kubbasi' because of the absence of a following vowel, saying they do not exist in Pali.

We, however, accept those forms because we see the method of the Pali texts. Here, to dispel the doubts of the listeners, I shall state some of the Pali methods:
'The virtuous do not do (evil); the fool performs (does) the precepts (virtues),' and,
'Why, venerable sir, do you resort to the secluded forest? He performs (does) ascetic practices here,' and,
'Performing (speaking) with harsh words.' (Such are the Pali passages).

In such places, the augment 'a'...
268:
(The augment 'a') should be made. Indeed, the method of the Pali texts is inconceivable and profound, and for the most part, it is far from the method of the grammar treatises. This is so because, just as the paradigm 'aggini (the fire), agginī (the fires), agginayo (the fires); agginiṃ (the fire), agginī (the fires), agginayo (the fires); aggininā (by the fire)' is to be made because of seeing the trend of the Pali text: "They enter the blazing fire," in the same way, the paradigm 'kubbati, kubbanti, kubbasi' should also be applied because of seeing the trend of the Pali text: "The fool performs bad habits."

And just as the paradigm 'sabbhi, sabbhī, sabbhayo; sabbhiṃ, sabbhī, sabbhayo; sabbhinā' is to be applied because of seeing the trend of the Pali text: "O Fire-god, this worship with the tail of an ox by the unrighteous has been much," and because of seeing the trend of the Commentary: "The virtuous, together with the virtuous, declare that the Dhamma of the virtuous does not reach decay," in the same way, the paradigm 'kubbati, kubbanti, kubbasi' should also be applied because of seeing the trend of the Pali text: "The fool performs bad habits." Likewise, all forms such as 'krubbati, krubbanti, krubbasi' should be applied in all places.

Now, the paradigm as promised has arrived. Karoti, karonti; karosi, karotha; karomi, kummi, karoma, kumma; kurute, kubbante; kuruse, kuruvhe; kare, karumhe. These are the forms stated by way of the present tense (vattamanā).

Karotu, kurutu, karontu; karohi, karotha; karomi, kummi, karoma, kumma; kurutaṃ, kubbantaṃ; karassu, kurussu, kuruvho; kare, kubbāmase. These are the forms stated by way of the imperative (pañcamī).

Regarding these imperative forms, someone might say:
"Marriage with the Nagas has never been done by us before.
Taṃ vivāhaṃ asaṃyuttaṃ, kathaṃ amhe karāmase — Why should we perform that marriage which is not suitable between Nagas and humans?"
269:
Looking at the trend of the Pali text, one might ask: Why is the word 'karomase' not mentioned here? Does not the 'ā' which is part of the 'āmase' suffix undergo elision depending on the 'o' following the root 'kar'? 

It is not so. This is because in the word 'karomase', the 'āmase' suffix is absent, and the 'ma' suffix is clearly present. In this word, the letter 'se' is an augment (āgama); therefore, the meaning should be taken according to the Vattamānā (Present) suffix as 'karomā', not according to the Pañcamī (Imperative) suffix. Such a 'se' augment also occurs after some nouns, for example: 'Ye keci buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gatāse' (Whoever has gone to the Buddha for refuge), 'Yaṃ balaṃ ahuvamhase' (Whatever strength there was), and so on. It also occurs after some verbs (ākhyāta) depending on the presence or absence of substitution (ādesa). For example: 'Akaramhase te kiccaṃ' (We have done your work), 'Okkantāmasi bhūtāni' (They respect the beings), 'Sutaṃ netaṃ abhiṇhaso, tasmā evaṃ vademase' (We have constantly heard this [worship] of the devas; therefore, we speak thus), and so on.

Forms expressed by the power of the Sattamī (Optative) suffix: kareyya, kareyyuṃ; kareyyāsi, kareyyātha; kareyyāmi, kareyyāma; kubbetha, kubberaṃ; kubbetho, kubbeyyavho; kareyyaṃ, kare, kareyyāmhe.

Forms expressed by the power of the Parokkhā (Perfect) suffix: kara, karu; kare, karittha; karaṃ, karimha; karittha, karire; karittho, karivho; kariṃ, karimhe.

Here, the word 'karā' should be construed with the Third Person (paṭhamapurisa) as 'The man did the work.' Also in 'Āguṃ kara mahārāja, akaraṃ kammadukkaṭaṃ', it should be construed with the Third Person as 'O Great King, you (Your Majesty) have committed a fault.' In this case, this usage becomes a Third Person usage, like 'Maññe bhavaṃ patthayati, rañño bhariyaṃ pativvataṃ' (I think Your Honor desires the Queen who is devoted to her husband), and so on.
270:
In the Jātaka Commentary, however, the Second Person (majjhimapurisa) usage is mentioned. 'Āguṃ karā' means 'O Great King, you have committed a great offense, a great evil.' 'Dukkaṭaṃ' means 'Whatever deed was done, it was ill-done; you have done that base deed.' Therefore, it should be understood that according to the Jātaka Commentary, 'kara', 'karī', and 'akaraṃ' can sometimes be Second Person usages.

Generally, however, they should be understood as Third Person (paṭhamapurisa) and First Person (uttamapurisa) usages, such as: 'Puriso kammaṃ kara' (The man did the work), 'Puriso kammaṃ karī' (The man did the work), 'Ahaṃ kammaṃ akaraṃ' (I did the work). Here, the form 'kara' is stated by the power of the aforementioned Parokkhā suffix, the form 'karī' by the power of the Ajjattanī (Aorist) suffix, and the form 'akaraṃ' by the power of the Hiyattanī (Imperfect) suffix. Among those, the word 'karittho' is used as the Second Person singular of the Parokkhā Attanopada, similar to the word 'kisittho' in the context: 'Seek another husband apart from me; do not become emaciated.' This method should be applied appropriately in other cases as well.

There are also forms: akā, akarā, akara (short vowel), and akaru. Here, the word 'akā' in the context 'Sabbārivijayaṃ akā' (He achieved victory over all enemies) is an example. 'Akarā' should be understood as a Third Person usage expressing a past action, as in 'The man did the work.' Indeed, the Pali text is seen: 'Rajjassa kira so bhīto, akarā ālaye bahū' (Fearing kingship, he made many pretenses). In the phrase 'Mā metaṃ akarā kammaṃ, mā me udakamāharī' (Do not do this deed for me, do not fetch water for me), although it is a Third Person usage expressing the past, because of the association with the word 'mā', the Hiyattanī and Ajjattanī suffixes do not express a specific time in the sense of the Pañcamī (Imperative) suffix, and they become suitable for Second Person usage as 'You, do not do; do not fetch'.

Furthermore, in 'Jarādhammaṃ mā jīrīti alabbhaneyyaṃ ṭhānaṃ' (The state of being subject to old age—may it not grow old—is an unattainable thing), etc., although it is a Third Person usage expressing the past, because of the association with the word 'mā', the Ajjattanī suffix has no specific time in the sense of the Pañcamī suffix, meaning 'May it not grow old'...
271:
...they become suitable for Third Person usage. Therefore, the teachers of the Commentaries said: 'Jarādhammaṃ mā jīrī means: that which is my nature of aging, may it not age. This method applies to the rest as well.' Regarding what we said, 'There is also the short-vowel reading akara', its existence should be known by the power of this Pali: 'Atikara'makara'cariya, mayhampe taṃ na ruccati' (Teacher, you have done an excessive deed; this does not please me). The meaning of that Pali should be taken according to the Third Person as 'Teacher, Your Honor has done an excessive deed.' Moreover, since the word 'you (tvaṃ)' is indeed what is meant when the word 'Your Honor (bhavaṃ)' is used, the construction 'Teacher, you are doing an excessive deed' should also be made according to the intention.

Akaro, akattha, akaroṭha. Akaraṃ, akaṃ, akaramha, akamha. Here, the Pali 'Saṃvaḍḍhitvā puḷinaṃ, akaṃ puḷinacetiyaṃ' (Having increased the sand, they made a sand stupa) is an example. Akattha, akatthuṃ. Akurushe, akaravhaṃ. Akariṃ, akaraṃ, akaramhase. These are forms stated by the power of the Hiyattanī suffix.

Here, five types of the letter 'se' should be brought forth and shown. Thus, there are five types of the letter 'se': as a part of a word (padāvayava), not as a part of a word (apadāvayava), as an indeterminate part of a word (anekantapadāvayava), having the meaning of the word 'so' (sossaddattha), and as a substitute (ādesa). Among those five, the letter 'se' as a part of a word is to be understood in 'Tvaṃ kammaṃ kuruse' (You do the work), 'Tvaṃ atthakusalo abhavase' (You have become skilled in the goal), and so on. The letter 'se' that is not a part of a word is to be understood in 'Tasmā evaṃ vademase' (Therefore we speak thus), 'Mūlā akusalā samūhatāse' (The unwholesome roots are uprooted), and so on. The letter 'se' as an indeterminate part of a word is to be understood in 'Arogā ca bhavāmase' (May we be free from disease), 'Maṇiṃ tāta gaṇhāmase' (Dear son, let us take the gem), and so on. Here, if the letter 'se' were a part of the 'āmase' suffix in the Pañcamī (Imperative) tense, then it would be a part of the words 'bhavāmase' and 'gaṇhāmase' which have the meanings of wishing and blessing associated with the Pañcamī suffix. If, however, it is an augment (āgama), it is not a part of the words 'bhavāma' and 'gaṇhāma' which have the meanings of wishing and blessing associated with the Pañcamī suffix. Thus...
272:
In words such as "bhavāmase", it should be understood that the letter "se" is not necessarily an integral part of the word. The letter "se" having the meaning of the word "so" should be seen in the phrase "esese eke ekatthe". The meaning of this word "esese" is "eso so eko ekattho" (This Ariya Vinaya is indeed that Sappurisa Vinaya; they have the same meaning). The letter "se" as an ādesa (substitution) should be understood in the phrase "akaramhasa te kiccaṃ" and also in "okkantamasi bhūtānī", by way of substituting the letter "e" with "a" and "i". Therein, the meaning of the word "akaramhasa te kiccaṃ" is "akaramhase te kiccaṃ". In this word "akaramhase", if the letter "se" were an āgama (augment), then the word "akarāmha" would be a word ending in the Hiyattanī Parassapada 1st person plural. If it were a part of the "mhase" termination, then the word "akaramhase" would be a word ending in the Hiyattanī Attanopada 1st person plural. Thus, it should be noted that there are five types of the letter "se".

akari, kari, akāsi, akaruṃ, akariṃsu, akaṃsu, akaṃsuṃ. akaro, akarittha, akāsittha.

Here also, the word "akaro" should be construed as "tvaṃ akaro" (you did). The word "akaro" should be regarded like the word "ado" which has the sense of the 2nd person singular in the phrase "varañce me ado sakkā". This is because, although it is not explicitly present in the Pāḷi text, it should be taken by way of method. However, the teachers desire the 2nd person form "akāsī" in the place where "akaro" is mentioned. Such a word usually belongs to the 3rd person. Indeed, many 3rd person Pāḷi passages such as "adāsi me, akāsi me" are seen. But in places such as "mākāsi mukhasā pāpaṃ, mā kho sūkaramukho ahူ", because of the association with the word "mā", it should be understood that the construction should be "tvaṃ pāpaṃ mā akāsi" (do not do evil), "mā sūkaramukho ahosi" (do not become one with a pig's face).
273:
akariṃ, kariṃ, akāsiṃ (I did); akariṃha, kariṃha, akāsiṃha (we did). akarā, akarū (did/have done). akaruse, akariwha (did/have done). akaraṃ, akariṃhe (did/have done). These are the forms expressed by the power of the Ajjattanī tense.

karissati (will do), karissanti (they will do). karissasi, karissatha. karissāmi, karissāma. karissate, karissante. karissase, karissawhe. karissaṃ (I shall do); there is also "kassaṃ". Thus, the Pāḷi "kassaṃ purisakāriyaṃ" (I shall perform the manly effort) is evident. karissāmhe. Likewise: kāhati, kāhanti. kāhasi, kāhatha. kāhāmi, kāhāma. kāhiti, kāhinti. kāhisi, and so on, should be construed as appropriate. These are the forms expressed by the power of the Bhavissantī tense.

akariṃsā, akariṃsa, akariṃsaṃsu, and so forth—all the rest should be construed accordingly. These are the forms expressed by the power of the Kālatipatti tense.

kayirati (does), kayiranti (they do). kayirasi, kayirātha. kayirāmi, kayirāma. kayirate. The rest should be construed. These are the forms expressed by the power of the Vattamānā tense.

kayiratu (let him do), kayirantu (let them do). The rest should be construed. These are the forms expressed by the power of the Pañcamī mood.

kayirā, kuyirā (should do). kayiruṃ (they should do). Here, there is this Pāḷi: "kumbhimhipañjaliṃ kuyirā, cātañcāpi padakkhiṇaṃ" (One should pay homage even to a full water-pot, and one should also perform a circumambulation around a blue jay). In that Pāḷi, the word-split should be "kumbhimhipi añjaliṃ". kayirāsi, kayirātha. kayirāmi, kayirāma. kayiretha, kayireraṃ. kayiretho, kayirāwho. kayiraṃ, kayirāmhe. These are the forms expressed by the power of the Sattamī mood.

Among those forms, this word "kayirā" should be construed by the power of the 3rd person, according to the finding: "puññañce puriso kayirā" (If a man should do merit). Also in the phrase "adhammaṃ sārathi kayirā", [it means] "the noble charioteer should do unrighteousness"...
274:
...should do", thus it should be construed by the power of the 3rd person only, and not by the power of the 2nd person. Or else, it should be understood that when "kayirāsi" should have been said, the letter "si" was elided and "kayirā" was spoken as a 2nd person form.

In this regard, there might be this objection: In the Pāḷi "puttaṃ labhetha varadaṃ", the Commentators did not take the meaning of this word "labhetha" by way of the 3rd person—as in "sabbhireva samāsetha, sabbhi kubbetha santhavaṃ" and so on—but having made a purisavipallāsa (exchange of person), they took the meaning as "labheyyaṃ" by way of the 1st person. Similarly, in this phrase "adhammaṃ sārathi kayirā", should you not also make a purisavipallāsa of the word "kayirā" and state the meaning as "kareyyāsi" by way of the 2nd person? And did the Commentators not also state that meaning as "kareyyāsi"?

It is true. Even though that is so, because the Commentators were endowed with supreme skill in conventional meanings, they considered that the word "bhavaṃ" (venerable/sir) occurs in the sense where "tvaṃ" (you) should be said, and the word "tvaṃ" occurs in the sense where "bhavaṃ" should be said. Thus, they stated the meaning as "kareyyāsi" by the power of the intended meaning (adhippāyattha), and not by way of purisavipallāsa. Indeed, in the Commentary on this verse "puttaṃ labhetha varadaṃ", having cited "labhetha", the explanation was made as "labheyyaṃ" by way of purisavipallāsa. However, in the Commentary on this verse "adhammaṃ sārathi kayirā", having cited "kayirā", the explanation was made as "kareyyāsi". Therefore, in this place "adhammaṃ sārathi kayirā", purisavipallāsa should not be considered.

Alternatively, in this place "puttaṃ labhetha varadaṃ", as well as in "kāye rajo na limphetha" and so on, the "etha" termination is taken. Instead of taking the "etha" termination like this, the word-split should be made as "labhe atha". If this is done, there is no need for purisavipallāsa. Therein, "labhe" means...
275:
The first person (uttamapurisa) of the optative mood (sattami) is as in the word "vajjhañcāpi pamocaye" (I would release even those deserving of death). The word "atha" is either a particle (nipāta) used in the sense of taking another object (a boon), or it is a verse-filler. In this context, by virtue of another object, it means "I would like to obtain another son as a boon." Since two meanings are seen to arise here, and since the Buddha's intention among these two is difficult to know, both meanings should be taken.

In this regard, although the six types of permutations (vipallāsa)—namely, permutation of gender (liṅga), case (vibhatti), number (vacana), tense (kāla), person (purisa), and letter (akkhara)—should be extracted and shown, they are not shown here because they will become clear later. Therein, the word "kayirātha" is divided into two types by virtue of the active voice (parassapada) and the middle voice (attanopada) of the optative mood; likewise, it is divided into two by virtue of the second person plural (majjhimapurisa bahuvacana) and the first person singular (paṭhamapurisa ekavacana). For instance, in the passage "yathā puññāni kayirātha, dadantā aparāparaṃ," the word "kayirātha" is spoken by virtue of the active voice of the optative and the second person plural. It means "you should perform meritorious deeds as appropriate." However, in the passage "kayirātha dhīro puññāni," the word "kayirātha" is spoken by virtue of the middle voice of the optative and the third person singular. It means "he should perform." Here, forms accompanied by the suffix "yira" by virtue of the perfect tense (parokkhā) etc., are mostly not well-known in the Dispensation (Sāsana), so they are not shown.

It is called "kāraṇa" because it performs its own fruit. It is called "kattā" (agent) because it performs. Likewise, it is called "kāraka" or "kārakaṃ." In this context, when the word "kāraka" expresses the agent (kattu-kāraka), the object (kamma-kāraka), etc., it is masculine and mostly also neuter. However, when it expresses a goldsmith (rajatakāra), a blacksmith (kammakāra), or a coppersmith (lohakāra), etc., it is exclusively masculine. It is called "kārāpaka" because it causes to perform. Karaṃ, kubbaṃ, kruvbaṃ, karonto, kubbanto, kubbāno, kurumāno (one who performs).
276:
Afflicting. A woman who performs (kārikā), a woman who causes to perform (kārāpikā). A woman who performs (karontī), a woman who performs (kubbantī). A family that performs (kārakaṃ kulaṃ). One who causes to perform (kārāpakaṃ), one who performs (karontaṃ), one who performs (kubbantaṃ), one who performs (kurumānaṃ). Saṅkhāra (formation/conditioning), parikkhāra (requisite), parikkhata (prepared/encircled), purakkhata (honoured/placed in front), karaṇa (doing/instrument), kriyā (action). Grammarians also desire the word "kriyā." In this regard, although words containing the consonant cluster of 'ka' and 'ra' are seen in passages such as "akrubbato aphalā hoti," the word "kriyā" is not prominent in the Pali Canon like the word "klesa." Even though it is not prominent, it should be accepted because it has been used by great teachers such as the Commentators. For this reason, word arrangements such as "kriyākriyāpattivibhāgadesako" are seen.

To do (kātuṃ), to do (kattuṃ). To do (kātave), to cause to do (kāretuṃ). Having done (katvā), having done (katvāna), having done (kātuna), having done (karitvā), having done (karitvāna), having done (kacca), having done excessively (adhikacca), having done (kariya), having done (kariyāna), having placed in front (purakkhitvā), having caused to do (kāretvā). Other suffixes like 'tumaṃ' should also be joined.

Among those words, "kacca" means having done. "Adhikacca" means having done excessively. Grammarians, relying on the methods of grammar treatises, desire the form "adhikicca," but we do not desire it because such a form is not in accordance with the Pali Canon. For this reason, in the Therīgāthā, in the words spoken by Great Mother Gotamī near her Parinibbāna, the Pali "padakkhiṇaṃ kacca nipacca pāde" is found. In that Pali, it means "having performed the circumambulation." By seeing the word "kacca," the word "adhikacca" is also already seen. This method should be understood accordingly in other places as well.

Now I shall speak of the slight excellence of meaning associated with the root 'kar'—Taṇhaṅkara Buddha. Affliction (kāraṇā). Afflicting with harsh words that are unpleasant to the ear (pakrubbamāno). The Pali passages are "sante na kurute piyaṃ" (he does not endear himself to the virtuous). Among those, Taṇhaṅkaro is so called because he acts upon (removes) the craving and greed of those to be tamed. Or, because he is endowed with the physical body (rūpakāya) and the Dhamma body (dhammakāya), he causes the craving and love of the entire world for himself; thus he is called Taṇhaṅkara. Kāraṇā means affliction.
277:
In that word "Taṇhaṅkaro," he is called Taṇhaṅkara because he acts upon (destroys) the craving and greed of those to be tamed. Alternatively, because of his attainment of the physical body and the Dhamma body, he causes the craving and affection of the entire world towards himself; thus he is called Taṇhaṅkara. "Kāraṇā" means afflicting. "Pakrubbamāno" means afflicting. "Sante na kurute piyaṃ" means he does not make the virtuous ones his dear, desired, liked, and heart-pleasing ones. Alternatively, it means being a person who is loved, liked, and rejoiced, he does not associate with or attend upon the virtuous. In the sense of "he attends upon the king," those learned in grammar treatises say "he makes the king dear"; such a rare method should be well-noted in mind.

And here, I shall present the extraction of the meanings of the word "parikkhāra." In passages such as "parikkhāro: he is well-surrounded by the seven city-requisites," it refers to the retinue or surroundings (parivāra). In passages such as "the chariot has white coverings (parikkhāra), the axle is jhāna, and the wheel is energy," it refers to ornament (alaṅkāra). In passages such as "those life-requisites (parikkhāra) which should be gathered by a renunciant," it refers to equipment or constituents (sambhāra). In this regard, it is said:

By the wise who know the Dispensation, in the Sāsana,
The word "parikkhāra" is spoken of
As retinue, as ornament, and as equipment.

The root "jāgara" is used in the sense of the end of sleep (wakefulness). "Jāgaro" means he wakes. "Jāgaraṃ" means wakefulness. "Long is the night to the one who is awake."

These many roots belonging to the Tanādi group have been seen by me according to my strength. Having looked for other roots in the Suttas, you should accept them according to their meaning and logic.

## This is the Tanādi group.
278:
The six groups starting with Rudhādi, which possess various essential meanings, produce wisdom, and are the great delight of the wise, should be well-cultivated by those with noble aspirations, just as golden swans frequent a pure place.

## Thus, the seventeenth chapter named Rudhādisakka in the Saddanīti, composed for the proficiency of the wise in the usage of the Tipitaka together with its commentaries consisting of the nine factors, is completed.

## 18. Curādigaṇaparidīpana

After this Rudhādisakka, I shall speak of the eighth group named Curādi, which brings about many benefits.

The root cur is used in the sense of stealing (theyya). Thenanaṃ, theyyaṃ, and corikā mean stealing. In that sense of stealing, the root cur occurs. Coreti, corayati (he steals), coro (a thief), corī (a female thief), corikā (theft), coretuṃ, corayituṃ (to steal), coretvā, corayitvā (having stolen). The presence of the suffixes ṇe and ṇaya in the sense of the agent (kattu) is the characteristic of the Curādi group. In the causative (kārita) sense: corāpeti, corāpayati (he causes to steal), corāpetuṃ, corāpayituṃ (to cause to steal), corāpetvā, corāpayitvā (having caused to steal). In the passive (kamma) sense: wealth is stolen by thieves (corīyati), stolen wealth (coritaṃ dhanaṃ). This method applies everywhere.
279:
## Kakārantadhātu

The root lok is used in the sense of looking. Loketi, lokayati (he looks, he sees), oloketi, olokayati (he looks down), ulloketi, ullokayati (he looks up), apaloketi, apalokayati (he looks back), āloketi, ālokayati (he looks straight), viloketi, vilokayati (he looks sideways). Loko (world), āloko (light/radiance), lokanaṃ (looking), olokanaṃ (looking down), ullokanaṃ (looking up), ālokanaṃ (looking straight), vilokanaṃ (looking sideways), apalokanaṃ (looking back or asking permission), avalokanaṃ (turning the body to look). Oloketuṃ, olokayituṃ (to look down), oloketvā, olokayitvā (having looked down). In the causative (kārita) sense, however, forms such as "olokāpeti, olokāpayati, olokāpetuṃ, olokāpayituṃ, olokāpetvā, olokāpayitvā" and so on should be applied. This method is the same in all instances.

In that context (the word loka), there are three types of loka: the world of formations (saṅkhāraloka), the world of beings (sattaloka), and the world of space (okāsaloka). Among these three, in the passage where it occurs as "The world is one; all beings subsist on nutriment," it should be understood as the world of formations. In the passage where it occurs as "The world is eternal" or "The world is not eternal," it is the world of beings.

"As far as the sun and moon revolve,
Shining and illuminating the quarters,
So far the world extends a thousandfold;
Therein your power is exercised."
In the passage where this occurs, it should be understood as the world of space.

Alternatively, loka is of three types: the world of defilements (kilesaloka), the world of existence (bhavaloka), and the world of faculties (indriyaloka). Therein, because of the abundance of defilements such as greed, beings of the sense sphere are called the world of defilements. Because of development through jhāna and direct knowledge, beings of the fine-material sphere are called the world of existence. Because of the abundance of imperturbable concentration and having pure faculties, beings of the immaterial sphere are called the world of faculties. Alternatively, defilement (kilesa) means that which torments; it means the suffering of the result (vipāka-dukkha). Therefore, because of the abundance of the suffering of result, beings in the woeful states are called the world of defilements. Other beings, because of the state of attainment in existence, are called the world of existence. Among them, those beings who are endowed with the faculties that mature into liberation should be understood as the world of faculties.

In the Jātaka Commentary, however:
280:
"The world is of many kinds: the world of formations, the world of beings, the world of space, the world of aggregates, the world of sense bases, and the world of elements. Herein, in the passage 'The world is one; all beings subsist on nutriment... the eighteen worlds are the eighteen elements,' the world of formations is spoken of. The world of aggregates and so on are included within that world of formations. In passages such as 'This world, the other world, the Brahma world together with the devas,' the world of beings is spoken of. In the passage 'As far as the sun and moon revolve, shining and illuminating the quarters; so far the world extends a thousandfold, therein your power is exercised,' the world of space is spoken of," so it is said.

In terms of meaning, however, the collection or the continuity of the aggregates connected with the faculties is the world of beings. One is called a 'being' (satta) because of being attached (satta/visatta) to forms and so on. In this being, wholesome and unwholesome [actions] and their results are established; therefore, it is called loka. The collection or the continuity of forms not connected with the faculties is the world of space. In this place, the trembling ones (tasa - worldlings and trainees) and the firm ones (thāvara - Arahants) reside; it is also the place where they reside; therefore, it is called the world of space. Because it is the receptacle for those beings, that world of space is also called the "world of the vessel" (bhājanaloka).

These two types of world are also "concepts based on [realities]" (upādāpaññatti) because they are designated depending on phenomena such as form, and thus they are not of the nature of ultimate reality (paramattha). Nevertheless, because they are designated depending on mental and material phenomena together with their causes, the nature of being dependent on causes is figuratively attributed to both the world of beings and the world of space through the power of the beings who grasp and the space that is grasped. The aggregates within these two worlds (beings and space) are called the world of formations. They are called formations (saṅkhāra) because they are conditioned by causes. They are called loka because they disintegrate (lujjanati). In this world of formations, although the Path and Fruit phenomena also have the nature of disintegration because they arise depending on causes, they do not attain the status of loka because only the phenomena belonging to the three planes are intended as "the world." For that very reason, they are called "supramundane" (lokuttara).

Āloka means radiance. People see intensely by means of this, or it sees the eye-consciousness; therefore, it is called āloka.
281:
Olokana means looking down. Vilokana means looking up. Ālokana means looking straight ahead. Vilokana means looking to both sides or various kinds of looking. Apalokana means informing, as in "having informed the Saṅgha" and so on. Avalokana means looking back by turning the front of the body, as in "having looked with the elephant-look" and so on. In the passage "He is one who acts with clear comprehension in looking ahead and looking aside (ālokite vilokite)," the meanings of ālokana and vilokana should also be taken as ālokita and vilokita by way of the abstract noun (bhāva).

The root thak- is used in the sense of closing or obstructing. A man closes the door; it is used as thaketi or thakayati.

The root takk- is used in the sense of thinking or pondering. It is used as takketi, vitakketi, or vitakkayati. There are terms such as takko, vitakko, and vitakkitā.

Among those two, thinking is called takko, which means the sense of ūhana (pondering); vitakko is the same. Alternatively, it is called vitakko because by this [mental factor] they think, or it thinks by itself, or it is merely the act of thinking. In the Abhidhamma, synonymous terms are stated as: "takka, vitakka, appanā, vyappanā, the directing of the mind onto an object (cetaso abhiniropanā)." One who thinks is called vitakkitā; this refers to a person. There is a Pali passage: "Those who are lazy and without thought (avitakkitā) go to death."

The root aki- is used in the sense of marking. Lakkhaṇa means a sign (saññāṇa), meaning the cause of recognition. Here, this point should be noted: In this Curādigana, those roots that have multiple vowels, no conjunct consonants, and are indicated by the indicatory letter 'i' (ikārānubandha), when they reach the state of a verb or a noun, they certainly result in forms produced by the arrival of the niggahīta (nasalization); they never appear in forms without the niggahīta. They are used as aṅketi, aṅkayati. Aṅkanaṃ (marking).
282:
Aṅko (a mark). In compounds, however, forms such as "the moon which has the rabbit-mark (sasaṅko)" and "the Buddha whose feet are marked with the wheel-sign (cakkaṅkitacaraṇo)" occur.

The roots sakk- and vakk- are used in the sense of speaking or shining. They are used as sakketi, sakkayati, vakketi, and vakkayati.

The roots nakk- and vakk- are used in the sense of perishing or destruction. They are used as nakketi, nakkayati, vakketi, and vakkayati.

The roots cakk- and cukk- are used in the sense of oppressing or harming. They are used as cakketi, cakkayati, cukketi, and cukkayati. Cakkaṃ (wheel/circle). For what reason is it called cakka? It is called cakka in the sense of being able to oppress or destroy.

The word cakka is found in the senses of: sampatti (attainment/prosperity), lakkhaṇa (mark), chariot wheel, iriyāpatha (posture), dāna (giving), ratana (gem), dhamma-cakka (Wheel of Dhamma), khura-cakka (razor-wheel), and so on.

In passages such as "Monks, there are these four wheels (blessings) for gods and humans who are endowed with them," this word cakka is found in the sense of sampatti. In "Wheel-marks appeared on the soles of the feet," it is found in the sense of lakkhaṇa. In "As the wheel follows the hoof of the ox that draws the load," it is found in the sense of a chariot part (wheel). In "Having four wheels and nine gates," it is found in the sense of postures (iriyāpatha). In "Give, enjoy, and be not negligent; turn the wheel of giving to living beings," it is found in the sense of dāna. In "The celestial wheel-gem appeared," it is found in the sense of a gem-wheel. In "The Wheel of Dhamma set in motion by me," it is found in the sense of the Dhamma-cakka. In "The razor-wheel revolves on the head of the person overcome by desire," it is found in the sense of a khura-cakka (razor-wheel). In "Even with a wheel having razor edges," it is found in the sense of a weapon-wheel. In "Asanivicakka," it is found in the sense of a circle of lightning.
283:
The root Taki is in the sense of binding. The forms are taṅketi, taṅkayati.

The root Akka is in the sense of praising. Thavana means praise (thuti). The forms are akketi, akkayati. Akko. The word Akko refers to the sun. Because that sun has great radiance, it is called 'Akka' because it is greatly praised by people who are devoted to it. Accordingly, for that sun, great praise is seen such as: "There is no radiance equal to the sun; this one-king with eyes has arisen."

The root Hikka is in the sense of harming. The forms are hikketi, hikkayati.

The root Nikka is in the sense of measuring (dimension). The forms are nikketi, nikkayati.

The root Bukka is in the sense of barking. Here, barking should be taken only as the barking of a dog, not as barking in the sense of speech. The forms are bukketi, bukkayati. Here, the worldly usage "The dog barks at the thief" (bukkayati sā core) should be known. In the Bhūvādi-gaṇa, however, the form is "bukkati sā." Another teacher reads it as "Bukka paribhasane"; even when reading it thus, only the barking of a dog is intended.

The roots Daka and Laka are in the sense of enjoyment. The forms are daketi, dakayati, laketi, lakayati.

The roots Takka and Loka are in the sense of speaking. The forms are takketi, takkayati, loketi, lokayati.

The roots Cika and Sika are in the sense of touching (handling). The forms are ciketi, cikayati, siketi, sikayati.

## Kakārantadhāturūpāni.
## Khakārantadhātu

The root Lakkha is in the sense of seeing and marking. Dassana means seeing (passana). Aṅka means a mark (lañzana). The forms are lakkheti, lakkhayati, sallakkheti, sallakkhayati. One shoots the target with an arrow; one makes a mark.
284:
The sands of the Gaṅgā may be exhausted, the water of the great ocean may be exhausted, the fine soil of the earth may be exhausted, but my wisdom cannot be exhausted by such measurement.

Characteristics of an aeon (or the Kappa treatise). Characteristics of a cow. Characteristics of a woman. Characteristics of phenomena (dhammas). Proper marking. Close marking. Direct close marking. In the forms of the root Lakkh ending with the suffix yu and preceded by prefixes such as saṃ-, the letter na is dental (dantaja).
